# Meléndez–Quiñónez dynasty

The **Meléndez–Quiñónez dynasty** (Spanish: *Dinastía Meléndez-Quiñónez*) refers to a succession of presidencies in El Salvador from 1913 to 1927, during which the executive power was held by members of the Meléndez and Quiñónez families. The period is characterized by the oligarchic rule of the landowning elite, specifically the coffee oligarchy, and the rotation of the presidency between two brothers, Carlos and Jorge Meléndez, and their brother-in-law, Alfonso Quiñónez Molina .

Rising to power following the assassination of President Manuel Enrique Araujo in 1913, the dynasty maintained control through a combination of electoral manipulation, the establishment of the National Democratic Party (PND), and the use of the *Liga Roja* (Red League), a paramilitary organization designed to suppress opposition and mobilize support . The era is noted for economic policies that favored the coffee industry, the negotiation of significant foreign loans, and the formulation of the "Meléndez Doctrine" regarding sovereignty in the Gulf of Fonseca . The dynasty's direct control over the government ended in 1927 when their chosen successor, Pío Romero Bosque, initiated democratic reforms and broke away from their influence .

## Establishment and Consolidation

The dynasty's origins lie in the political vacuum created by the assassination of President Manuel Enrique Araujo on February 9, 1913. Carlos Meléndez, a wealthy landowner and politician who had been named the first presidential designate, assumed the provisional presidency following the resignation of Vice President Onofre Durán Santillana .

To consolidate power and legitimize their rule, the family utilized the National Democratic Party (*Partido Nacional Democrático*, PND). The succession of power was managed within the family unit: Carlos Meléndez served until 1918 (with a brief interlude by Quiñónez to allow for Carlos's election), followed by his brother Jorge Meléndez (1919–1923), and finally their brother-in-law Alfonso Quiñónez Molina (1923–1927) .

### The Triumvirate
The dynasty was primarily led by three individuals:
* **Carlos Meléndez (1861–1919):** The initiator of the dynasty, he served as provisional president (1913–1914) and constitutional president (1915–1918). His administration focused on maintaining neutrality during World War I and opposing the Bryan-Chamorro Treaty .
* **Jorge Meléndez (1871–1953):** The younger brother of Carlos, he served as president from 1919 to 1923. His tenure was marked by economic volatility and the suppression of political opposition .
* **Alfonso Quiñónez Molina (1874–1950):** A physician and politician married to Leonor Meléndez (sister of Carlos and Jorge). He served as provisional president on multiple occasions and as constitutional president from 1923 to 1927. He is often credited as the intellectual architect behind the dynasty's political machinery, including the *Liga Roja* .

## Political Repression and the *Liga Roja*

A defining feature of the Meléndez–Quiñónez era was the creation and utilization of the *Liga Roja* (Red League) in 1918. Founded by Alfonso Quiñónez Molina, the League was ostensibly a labor organization designed to mediate between the government and the peasantry. However, historians describe it as a paramilitary apparatus used to manipulate elections, intimidate political opponents, and enforce the dynasty's will .

The League operated with the support of the National Guard and the army, effectively monopolizing political activity. It played a crucial role in ensuring the election of Jorge Meléndez in 1919 and Alfonso Quiñónez in 1923 by suppressing rival political movements . While it employed vague socialist rhetoric to appeal to the working class, it ultimately served the interests of the coffee oligarchy .

### Christmas Day Massacre (1922)
The repression exercised by the dynasty culminated in the Christmas Day Massacre (*Masacre de Navidad*) on December 25, 1922. During the presidential campaign for the 1923 elections, women supporting the opposition candidate Miguel Tomás Molina organized a demonstration in San Salvador. They marched to protest the arrest of opposition figures and to demand fair elections .

Security forces and members of the *Liga Roja* opened fire on the demonstrators near the El Calvario church and the Central Market. The attack resulted in an unspecified number of deaths and injuries among the women and other protesters . Following the massacre, Miguel Tomás Molina fled the country, and Alfonso Quiñónez Molina ran unopposed, winning the presidency with 100% of the reported vote .

## Economic Policies and Foreign Relations

The economic policies of the Meléndez–Quiñónez dynasty were heavily oriented toward the export of coffee, which benefited the landowning elite but left the national economy vulnerable to fluctuations in global market prices.

### The 1922 Loan and Corruption Allegations
During the presidency of Jorge Meléndez, the country faced a severe fiscal crisis exacerbated by low coffee prices. In 1922, the government negotiated a controversial loan with American bankers to cover the deficit and pave the streets of San Salvador. The negotiation process was led by René Keilhauer, who acted as a representative for El Salvador while simultaneously being an employee of Minor Keith, the owner of the United Fruit Company and a representative of the lending banks .

The terms of the loan were considered onerous, compromising 70% of the nation's customs revenues to service the debt and allowing for the installation of a U.S. fiscal representative to oversee customs collections . This arrangement drew criticism for eroding national sovereignty and for the conflict of interest inherent in the negotiations .

### The Meléndez Doctrine
In foreign policy, the dynasty is noted for the "Meléndez Doctrine," formulated during the administration of Carlos Meléndez. This legal and diplomatic stance was a response to the Bryan-Chamorro Treaty (1914) between the United States and Nicaragua, which granted the U.S. rights to build a canal across Nicaragua and establish a naval base in the Gulf of Fonseca .

El Salvador argued that the Gulf of Fonseca was a historic bay under the co-ownership (*condominium*) of El Salvador, Honduras, and Nicaragua, and that Nicaragua lacked the right to unilaterally cede territory for a foreign naval base, which would threaten El Salvador's security . The Salvadoran government took the case to the Central American Court of Justice, which ruled in 1917 that the treaty violated El Salvador's rights. However, both Nicaragua and the United States ignored the ruling, contributing to the Court's eventual dissolution .

## Downfall

The dynasty's grip on power ended in 1927. Alfonso Quiñónez Molina, constitutionally barred from re-election, selected his Vice President and Minister of War, Pío Romero Bosque, as his successor. Quiñónez and the Meléndez family expected Romero Bosque to act as a puppet, allowing them to retain de facto control over the government .

Upon assuming the presidency on March 1, 1927, Romero Bosque broke with the dynasty. He lifted the state of siege, allowed for greater press freedom, and refused to be controlled by the Meléndez–Quiñónez family . In December 1927, Jorge Meléndez and Alfonso Quiñónez organized a coup attempt to overthrow Romero Bosque and restore their control. The coup failed, leading to the exile of the conspirators and the definitive end of the dynasty's political hegemony .

## Legacy

The Meléndez–Quiñónez dynasty represents the consolidation of the "Coffee Republic" in El Salvador, a period of relative political stability achieved through authoritarianism and the exclusion of the majority of the population from the political process . While the dynasty oversaw infrastructure modernization, such as the paving of San Salvador and the introduction of radio, its reliance on repression and the suppression of labor movements contributed to the social tensions that would erupt in the 1932 peasant uprising and subsequent massacre (*La Matanza*) .

Meléndez Family
===============

Meléndez family, a Salvadoran family that held the presidency for three consecutive terms (1913–1927) during the period known as the Meléndez-Quiñónez dynasty era. The Meléndez presidents' fourteen-year occupancy of the nation's highest office is the most obvious example of the restrictive, elitist nature of Salvadoran politics. The Meléndez clan was part of the original Salvadoran landowning oligarchy dating from the early nineteenth century. Originally producers of indigo, they were among the first to grow coffee on a large scale.

President Carlos Meléndez (_b._ 1 February 1861; _d._ 8 October 1918) took office in 1913 following the assassination of Manuel Araujo. He had made many trips to the [United States](https://www.encyclopedia.com/places/united-states-and-canada/us-political-geography/united-states) and wished to promote industrialization and the diversification of [El Salvador](https://www.encyclopedia.com/places/latin-america-and-caribbean/salvadoran-political-geography/el-salvador)'s agrarian economy into henequen and cotton. However, his tenure in office is most notable for two policies: his decision to keep [El Salvador](https://www.encyclopedia.com/places/latin-america-and-caribbean/salvadoran-political-geography/el-salvador) neutral in [World War I](https://www.encyclopedia.com/history/modern-europe/wars-and-battles/world-war-i), despite heavy pressure from the [United States](https://www.encyclopedia.com/places/united-states-and-canada/us-political-geography/united-states), and his claim to the Gulf of Fonseca as a condominium territory. The latter resulted in the issuing of the so-called Meléndez Doctrine, which challenged Nicaragua's right to grant the United States a naval base in the Gulf of Fonseca as stipulated by the Bryan-Chamorro Treaty of 1913. Meléndez took his case to the Central American Court of Justice in 1914 and won a judgment in his favor.

Carlos Meléndez passed the presidency to his younger brother Jorge (_b._ 15 April 1871; _d._ 22 November 1953) when his health failed in 1918. Jorge ruled for four turbulent years punctuated by military uprisings, urban labor protests, and demonstrations in [San Salvador](https://www.encyclopedia.com/places/latin-america-and-caribbean/salvadoran-political-geography/san-salvador). Of these, the most serious were a February 1922 revolt of students at the Military Polytechnic School and a popular demonstration in December of that same year which was put down by the army and police. Jorge Meléndez continued his brother's program of modernization by opening the first airport, announcing a campaign to eradicate illiteracy, and creating a monetary commission. However, Jorge Meléndez is remembered also for his increased usage of the Liga Roja (Red League), a shadowy paramilitary group designed to thwart labor organization.

The Meléndez's brother-in-law Alfonso Quiñones Molina was president from 1923 to 1927 and continued the same form of elite-dominated politics as his predecessors. The Meléndez-Quiñónez dynasty governed El Salvador during a crucial period in its modern history. In the 1980s, their descendant, Jorge Antonio Meléndez, fought with the People's Revolutionary Army (ERP) as part of the FMLN-FDR coalition against the government.

_See also_[**El Salvador**](https://www.encyclopedia.com/humanities/encyclopedias-almanacs-transcripts-and-maps/el-salvador-0) .

**Alfonso Quiñónez Molina** ([Suchitoto](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suchitoto "Suchitoto"); 11 de enero de 1874-[San Salvador](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Salvador "San Salvador"), 22 de mayo de 1950) fue un [político](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pol%C3%ADtico "Político") y [médico](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/M%C3%A9dico "Médico") salvadoreño, quien fue [Presidente de El Salvador](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presidente_de_El_Salvador "Presidente de El Salvador") en tres mandatos no consecutivos: de 1914 a 1915, de 1918 a 1919 y de 1923 a 1927. También se desempeñó como [Vicepresidente](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vicepresidente_de_El_Salvador "Vicepresidente de El Salvador") durante las administraciones de sus cuñados [Carlos Meléndez](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carlos_Mel%C3%A9ndez_/(pol%C3%ADtico/) "Carlos Meléndez (político)") (1915-1918) y [Jorge Meléndez](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jorge_Mel%C3%A9ndez "Jorge Meléndez") (1919-1923), convirtiéndose en la única persona que se ha desempeñado en tres diferentes ocasiones como Presidente, ya de forma provisoria o electo popularmente, y en dos ocasiones como Vicepresidente. Durante este mandato fundó la [Radio Nacional de El Salvador](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radio_Nacional_de_El_Salvador "Radio Nacional de El Salvador").

Fueron sus padres Lucio Quiñónez y Aurelia Molina de Quiñónez.

Se casó con Leonor Meléndez (hermana de [Carlos](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carlos_Mel%C3%A9ndez_/(pol%C3%ADtico/) "Carlos Meléndez (político)") y [Jorge Meléndez](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jorge_Mel%C3%A9ndez "Jorge Meléndez"), Presidentes de la República de El Salvador). De esta unión nació una hija llamada Mercedes Quiñónez Meléndez.

Esta familia fue destruida por las personas que asesinaron a su padre.

El 4 de marzo de 1914, la Asamblea Nacional lo proclamó [Primer Designado a la Presidencia](https://es.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Primer_Designado_a_la_Presidencia&action=edit&redlink=1 "Primer Designado a la Presidencia (aún no redactado)") de la República; fue Tercer Vocal Suplente de la Junta Directiva del manicomio; Catedrático de Higiene y Terapéutica de la [Universidad de El Salvador](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universidad_de_El_Salvador "Universidad de El Salvador"); Consejero Suplente de la Facultad de Medicina y luego Segundo Vocal de la Directiva y Director de la Profilaxis Venérea, Dirigió el Manicomio y [Asilo Sara](https://es.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Asilo_Sara&action=edit&redlink=1 "Asilo Sara (aún no redactado)"), donde hizo muchos bienes en estos centros. En 1909, el Supremo Gobierno de la República le confirió las credenciales de delegado a la Cuarta Conferencia Sanitaria Internacional, verificada en [San José](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Jos%C3%A9_/(Costa_Rica/) "San José (Costa Rica)"), [Costa Rica](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Costa_Rica "Costa Rica"). Gobernó durante los años de mayor auge cafetalero.

### Presidencias de Alfonso Quiñónez Molina

\[[editar](https://es.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Alfonso_Qui%C3%B1%C3%B3nez_Molina&action=edit&section=3 "Editar sección: Presidencias de Alfonso Quiñónez Molina")\]

[![Image 4](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d6/1ST_PAN_AMERICAN_FINANCIAL_CONFERENCE%2C_WASHINGTON%2C_D.C.%2C_MAY_1915._SALVADOREAN_DELEGATION-_ROBERTO_ANGLIAE%3B_ALFONSO_GUINONES_LCCN2016866418.jpg/250px-1ST_PAN_AMERICAN_FINANCIAL_CONFERENCE%2C_WASHINGTON%2C_D.C.%2C_MAY_1915._SALVADOREAN_DELEGATION-_ROBERTO_ANGLIAE%3B_ALFONSO_GUINONES_LCCN2016866418.jpg)](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archivo:1ST_PAN_AMERICAN_FINANCIAL_CONFERENCE,_WASHINGTON,_D.C.,_MAY_1915._SALVADOREAN_DELEGATION-_ROBERTO_ANGLIAE;_ALFONSO_GUINONES_LCCN2016866418.jpg)

Quiñónez Molina gobernó durante los años de mayor auge cafetalero, junto al ministro de Hacienda, José Esperanza Suay.

Cuñado de Carlos y [Jorge Meléndez](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jorge_Mel%C3%A9ndez "Jorge Meléndez"), recibió la presidencia provisional el 29 de agosto de 1914 y la entregó el 1 de marzo de 1915, tras las elecciones que darían por ganador a su antecesor. Tras la renuncia de su cuñado Carlos, volvió a recibir el cargo provisional el 21 de diciembre de 1918, entregándolo el 1 de marzo de 1919. Retomó el cargo tras ganar unas elecciones, las cuales lo colocaron como presidente del 1 de marzo de 1923 al 1 de marzo de 1927.En las elecciones de 1922 se volvieron a reactivar las ligas rojas para la campaña electoral en la que iba como candidato oficial Alfonso Quiñónez Molina; teniendo como principal opositor a Miguel Tomás Molina del Partido Constitucional. Las ligas rojas tenían un jefe, seguido de jefes de barrios y jefes cantonales (que afiliaban a los vecinos); en el departamento de Sonsonate la mayoría de sus miembros eran indígenas, en Izalco había dos jefes siendo uno de ellos Feliciano Ama. Esta campaña se caracterizó por ser extremadamente violenta, el 22 de diciembre de 1922 una manifestación de mujeres a favor de Miguel Tomás Molina fue sofocada a disparos de fusil y ametralladora. Al final Miguel Tomás Molina se retiró y la elección fue ganada por Quiñónez.[\[1\]](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfonso_Qui%C3%B1%C3%B3nez_Molina#cite_note-FOOTNOTEL%C3%B3pez_Bernal2015El_Salvador_en_el_mundo-1)​[\[2\]](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfonso_Qui%C3%B1%C3%B3nez_Molina#cite_note-FOOTNOTEL%C3%B3pez_Bernal2015La_vida_pol%C3%ADtica-2)​[\[3\]](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfonso_Qui%C3%B1%C3%B3nez_Molina#cite_note-3)​[\[4\]](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfonso_Qui%C3%B1%C3%B3nez_Molina#cite_note-:30-4)​

[![Image 5](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/53/Christmas_Day_Massacre_%28El_Salvador%29.jpg/250px-Christmas_Day_Massacre_%28El_Salvador%29.jpg)](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archivo:Christmas_Day_Massacre_/(El_Salvador/).jpg)

Masacre del 25 de diciembre de 1922 en las cercanías entre la iglesia El Calvario y el Mercado Central en [San Salvador](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Salvador "San Salvador").

En el mandato como presidente electo de Alfonso Quiñónez Molina, buscando limar las asperezas pasadas y aumentar su popularidad, disolvió las ligas rojas, aunque mantuvo el estado de sitio impuesto por su predecesor. Asimismo, buscó ampliar la esfera de acción del Estado a través de la modernización de la infraestructura, diversificación de la actividad agrícola, modernización de la burocracia estatal, y reorientación del sistema educativo nacional. Durante su gobierno se pavimentó la ciudad de San Salvador, se fundó la Flotilla aérea salvadoreña (hoy Fuerza aérea), se fundó la primera radio (llamada radio A.Q.M.). Es en este momento en que se organizan los primeros sindicatos sin que existiesen disposiciones legales.[\[5\]](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfonso_Qui%C3%B1%C3%B3nez_Molina#cite_note-FOOTNOTECastro_Mor%C3%A1n2005VI._La_Polic%C3%ADa_Nacional_en_los_a%C3%B1os_1900-1949-5)​[\[6\]](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfonso_Qui%C3%B1%C3%B3nez_Molina#cite_note-FOOTNOTELeistenschneiderLeistenschneider1980181-182-6)​[\[7\]](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfonso_Qui%C3%B1%C3%B3nez_Molina#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMaga%C3%B1a_Granados2000bA%C3%B1os_de_bonanza_y_crisis;_de_ilusiones_y_desencantos._1924-1931-7)​ [\[8\]](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfonso_Qui%C3%B1%C3%B3nez_Molina#cite_note-byv2-8)​

Durante su gestión, destaca la masacre a la primera manifestación femenina en el país. Esta manifestación terminó siendo reprimida por la [Guardia Nacional](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guardia_Nacional_/(El_Salvador/) "Guardia Nacional (El Salvador)") y La Liga Roja que era un grupo paramilitar creado por Quiñones para vigilar a la oposición la manifestación terminó con un saldo de [víctimas](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/V%C3%ADctimas "Víctimas") desconocido, algunas personas pudieron refugiarse en el hospicio de varones que colindaba con la iglesia el calvario, Quiñonez terminó ganando la elección tres semanas después en esta [manifestación](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manifestaci%C3%B3n "Manifestación") se destaca la participación de [Prudencia Ayala](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prudencia_Ayala "Prudencia Ayala") a los 37 años de edad.[\[9\]](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfonso_Qui%C3%B1%C3%B3nez_Molina#cite_note-cuscatla-9)​

El final de la dinastía Meléndez-Quiñones
-----------------------------------------

\[[editar](https://es.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Alfonso_Qui%C3%B1%C3%B3nez_Molina&action=edit&section=4 "Editar sección: El final de la dinastía Meléndez-Quiñones")\]

Alfonso Quiñonez Molina intentó buscar una reelección presidencial para el periodo 1927-1931, haciendo una reforma a la constitución de 1886, pero esta terminó fracasando por falta de tiempo, y como ya es costumbre prosiguió a darle el poder al Dr. [Pío Romero Bosque](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/P%C3%ADo_Romero_Bosque "Pío Romero Bosque"), quien era médico personal de la familia Quiñonez lo cual generó confianza para darle el cargo, Romero Bosque no era de las grandes familias cafetaleras del país, lo cual dio como uno de los pocos presidentes de corte independiente que obtienen el poder.

La dinastía Meléndez-Quiñones cedió la presidencia a [Pio Romero Bosque](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/P%C3%ADo_Romero_Bosque "Pío Romero Bosque"), quien fue electo el 1 de marzo de 1927 y que con anterioridad se había desempeñado como ministro de Guerra en las administraciones de Jorge Meléndez y Alfonso Quiñónez Molina, y vicepresidente en la última. Se pensaba que, al no ser miembro de una de las grandes familias latifundistas del país, el nuevo presidente sería una marioneta en sus manos.

[![Image 6](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b6/Miembros_del_Gabinete_y_Ejercito_del_Gobierno_del_Dr._Alfonso_Qui%C3%B1onez_Molina_%E2%80%93_1926.jpg/250px-Miembros_del_Gabinete_y_Ejercito_del_Gobierno_del_Dr._Alfonso_Qui%C3%B1onez_Molina_%E2%80%93_1926.jpg)](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archivo:Miembros_del_Gabinete_y_Ejercito_del_Gobierno_del_Dr._Alfonso_Qui%C3%B1onez_Molina_%E2%80%93_1926.jpg)

Miembros del Gabinete y Ejército del Gobierno del Dr. Alfonso Quiñonez Molina, a la derecha su sucesor Pio Romero Bosque.

Pero Romero Bosque desde el primer momento, dio muestras de su independencia; para mayo de 1927 había quitado el estado de sitio y concedió una amplia libertad de prensa y manifestación; asimismo, debido a protestas de los estudiantes de la Universidad Nacional, expulsó del país al expresidente y entonces primer designado a la presidencia Alfonso Quiñones Molina, quien fue a radicarse a Francia. Debido a ello, en diciembre de ese año, el expresidente Jorge Meléndez intentó llevar a cabo un golpe de Estado junto con algunos militares, liderados por el director de la maestranza del ejército Coronel Juan Enrique Aberle, el alto jefe de la Policía Nacional Mayor Manuel Alfaro Noguera y el jefe del primer regimiento de infantería Carlos Carmona Tadey. Sin embargo, dicha acción fue un rotundo fracaso; las fuerzas del gobierno capturaron a un total de 140 personas con pistolas y machetes, y un consejo de guerra extraordinario condenó a ser fusilados al Coronel Aberle y al Mayor Alfaro Noguera; mientras que el expresidente Meléndez logró escapar a Honduras para luego radicarse en Costa Rica.[\[10\]](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfonso_Qui%C3%B1%C3%B3nez_Molina#cite_note-10)​[\[11\]](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfonso_Qui%C3%B1%C3%B3nez_Molina#cite_note-Rese%C3%B1a_hist%C3%B3rica-11)​[\[12\]](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfonso_Qui%C3%B1%C3%B3nez_Molina#cite_note-12)​[\[13\]](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfonso_Qui%C3%B1%C3%B3nez_Molina#cite_note-:14-13)​

**Jorge Meléndez Ramírez** ([San Salvador](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Salvador "San Salvador"), 15 de abril de 1871-San Salvador, 22 de noviembre de 1953) fue un [político](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pol%C3%ADtico "Político") salvadoreño, quien fue [Presidente de El Salvador](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presidente_de_El_Salvador "Presidente de El Salvador") desde 1919 hasta 1923.

Fueron sus padres: Rafael Meléndez, hombre honrado de oficio sastre, casado con la distinguida señorita Mercedes Ramírez, (hija del [Norberto Ramírez](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norberto_Ram%C3%ADrez "Norberto Ramírez"), que fue presidente de El Salvador del 20 de septiembre de 1840 al 7 de enero de 1841, de origen Nicaragüense, y había sido Presidente también de la república de [Honduras](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Honduras "Honduras")).

Hermanos de Jorge Meléndez: Rafael, Francisco, Guillermo, Carmen de Letona y una [monja](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monja "Monja") [Sor](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sor "Sor") Meléndez; [Carlos](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carlos_Mel%C3%A9ndez_/(El_Salvador/) "Carlos Meléndez (El Salvador)") que fue presidente de El Salvador: 9 de febrero de 1913 a 29 de agosto de 1914 y 1.º de marzo de 1915 al 21 de diciembre de 1918, y Leonor (casada con [Alfonso Quiñónez Molina](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfonso_Qui%C3%B1%C3%B3nez_Molina "Alfonso Quiñónez Molina"), Presidente de la República de El Salvador: 29 de agosto de 1914 al 1 de marzo de 1915, 21 de diciembre de 1918 a 1 de marzo de 1919 y 1 de marzo de 1923 al 1 de marzo de 1927).

Fruto de su matrimonio con Tula Mazzini, nacieron 3 hijos: Jorge (falleció en plena juventud), María de los Ángeles y Ricardo.

[![Image 5: A black-and-white photograph of Jorge Meléndez surrounded by public workers](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/fc/Jorge_Mel%C3%A9ndez_in_1919.jpg/250px-Jorge_Mel%C3%A9ndez_in_1919.jpg)](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archivo:Jorge_Mel%C3%A9ndez_in_1919.jpg)

El presidente Jorge Meléndez con trabajadoras públicas en 1919.

Jorge Meléndez fue elegido por el período 1919-1923 y recibió la Presidencia de la República de su cuñado el [Alfonso Quiñónez Molina](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfonso_Qui%C3%B1%C3%B3nez_Molina "Alfonso Quiñónez Molina"), el 1 de marzo de 1919. Como vicepresidente, quedó el Dr. Quiñónez.

¿Por qué arriesgarían los capitalistas su dinero invirtiéndolo en un negocio de transporte, por ejemplo, cuando por la mañana el General X, jefe de una banda revolucionaria, lo expropia? ¿Por qué invertirían su dinero en empresas útiles cuando con la misma rapidez se lo extraen mediante un tributo exagerado decretado por algún gobierno irresponsable nacido entre el fragor de los disparos? \[...\] Es necesario que la política se guíe por un camino que poco a poco elimine la gangrena del personalismo, causa primordial de nuestra inestabilidad.

—14 de septiembre de 1917[\[1\]](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jorge_Mel%C3%A9ndez#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChing1997243-1)​

**Gobierno de Jorge Meléndez**

[![Image 6](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/66/%22Venecia%22_sugar_hacienda_in_El_Salvador_%284%29.png/250px-%22Venecia%22_sugar_hacienda_in_El_Salvador_%284%29.png)](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archivo:%22Venecia%22_sugar_hacienda_in_El_Salvador_/(4/).png)

La hacienda azucarera Venecia propiedad de Jorge Meléndez.[\[2\]](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jorge_Mel%C3%A9ndez#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWard1916222-2)​

La [Dinastía Meléndez Quiñonez](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dinast%C3%ADa_Mel%C3%A9ndez-Qui%C3%B1ones "Dinastía Meléndez-Quiñones") que inicio tras el asesinato del Presidente [Manuel Enrique Araujo](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manuel_Enrique_Araujo "Manuel Enrique Araujo") tenía la tradición de dar el cargo [presidencial](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presidencialismo "Presidencialismo") usando el [Nepotismo](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nepotismo "Nepotismo") como herramienta principal para dicha acción, la dinastía empezó con el presidente [Carlos Meléndez](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carlos_Mel%C3%A9ndez_/(pol%C3%ADtico/) "Carlos Meléndez (político)") un [latifundista](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latifundio "Latifundio") de las familias cafetaleras en [El Salvador](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Salvador "El Salvador"), que tras su [fallecimiento](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fallecimiento "Fallecimiento") su [hermano](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hermano "Hermano") Jorge Meléndez lo sustituyó en el cargo presidencial continuando las [políticas](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pol%C3%ADticas_p%C3%BAblicas "Políticas públicas") de su antecesor, Para 1922 Jorge Meléndez tuvo que enfrentar altos [escándalos](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Esc%C3%A1ndalos "Escándalos") de [corrupción](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corrupci%C3%B3n_pol%C3%ADtica "Corrupción política"), déficit económico, desastres naturales y bajos aumentos salariales a empleados públicos a la vez tuvo lidiar con la [deuda externa](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deuda_externa "Deuda externa") heredada de la [federación centroamericana](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Provincias_Unidas_del_Centro_de_Am%C3%A9rica "Provincias Unidas del Centro de América") fue así que el gobierno de Meléndez tuvo que hacer [millonarios](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Millonario "Millonario") [préstamos](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pr%C3%A9stamos "Préstamos") y [contratos de arrendamiento](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Contrato_de_arrendamiento "Contrato de arrendamiento") hacia los [puertos marítimos,](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Puerto "Puerto") y [transportes ferroviarios](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferroviario "Ferroviario") con durabilidad de 15 años hacia los [Bancos estadounidenses](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Banco "Banco") y la [United Fruit Company](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Fruit_Company "United Fruit Company"), esto provocó manifestaciones a nivel nacional las cuales terminaron siendo reprimidas por la [Policía Nacional](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cuerpos_de_Seguridad_/(El_Salvador/) "Cuerpos de Seguridad (El Salvador)"). A mediados de 1918, Jorge Meléndez (hermano menor de Carlos) y Quiñónez fundaron el Partido Nacional Demócrata (PND) para consolidar sus redes y alianzas políticas. Toda actividad política fuera del partido fue pronto ilegalizada. Durante la presidencia de Carlos, los hermanos Meléndez presentaron su gobierno y una ruptura con el pasado del país de violencia faccional y revoluciones. En un panfleto titulado "Orientaciones económicas del presidente Meléndez", Jorge elogió la presidencia de su hermano por haber derrotado...[\[3\]](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jorge_Mel%C3%A9ndez#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChing1997214_&_246-3)​ [caudillismo](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caudillo "Caudillo") En nombre de un "gobierno civilizado", presentaron esta imagen liberal y democrática del gobierno para justificar la centralización del poder en su gobierno, el Club Melendista y el PND. [\[4\]](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jorge_Mel%C3%A9ndez#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChing1997243%E2%80%93244-4)​ .[\[5\]](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jorge_Mel%C3%A9ndez#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChing1997246%E2%80%93247-5)​[\[6\]](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jorge_Mel%C3%A9ndez#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBernal_Ram%C3%ADrezQuijano_de_Batres200957%E2%80%9359-6)​En el período previo a las elecciones presidenciales de 1919 (Elecciones presidenciales salvadoreñas de 1919), Carlos no designó un sucesor presidencial, por lo que Quiñónez y Tomás García Palomo (el ministro de gobierno y finanzas de Carlos) se enfrentaron entre sí.[\[7\]](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jorge_Mel%C3%A9ndez#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChing1997244-7)​ Durante las elecciones municipales de diciembre de 1918, los partidarios de Quiñónez y Palomo se enfrentaron en los colegios electorales, con un saldo de unas 100 personas muertas y 200 heridas. Las elecciones resultaron en la victoria de los aliados de Quiñónez, lo que prácticamente le aseguró la victoria en las elecciones presidenciales.[\[8\]](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jorge_Mel%C3%A9ndez#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChing1997247%E2%80%93248-8)​El 21 de diciembre de 1918, Carlos renunció a la presidencia por enfermedad y Quiñónez asumió la presidencia, lo que lo descalificó para participar en las elecciones. Palomo posteriormente se retiró de la contienda porque no quería competir contra Quiñónez, ya que este consideraba presentarse de todos modos.[\[9\]](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jorge_Mel%C3%A9ndez#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChing1997248%E2%80%93249-9)​Una semana antes de las elecciones, Quiñónez seleccionó a Jorge como candidato del PND.[\[10\]](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jorge_Mel%C3%A9ndez#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChing1997249-10)​ [Arturo Araujo](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arturo_Araujo "Arturo Araujo") (quien no tiene parentesco con Manuel Enrique Araujo),[\[11\]](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jorge_Mel%C3%A9ndez#cite_note-FOOTNOTECastellanos200154-11)​ presidente del Partido Laborista Salvadoreño, también anunció su propia campaña. En respuesta, Jorge y Quiñónez ordenaron al presidente de la Corte Suprema de Justicia de El Salvador, Pío Romero Bosque, que se postulara, y planearon que recibiera más votos que Araujo para humillarlo. La elección resultó en que Meléndez obtuvo el 97% de los votos, Romero el 2% y Araujo el 1%.[\[12\]](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jorge_Mel%C3%A9ndez#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChing1997249%E2%80%93251-12)​

Después de tomar posesión el candidato oficial, Araujo y el General Juan Amaya intentaron una Revolución transfronteriza con el aparente apoyo del gobierno de Honduras, entraron a El Salvador con trescientos colaboradores. El ejército Salvadoreño los derrotó tras una dura batalla, y ellos tuvieron que replegarse en Honduras.<El Salvador Twentieth Century, Percy Falcke Martin, Longmans Green & Co. 1911>

En las elecciones presidenciales de 1919 hubo un fraude, encabezado por el clan Meléndez-Quiñonez, quienes establecieron el control político sobre todo el país. Después de las elecciones que fueron robadas, la Guardia Nacional fue enviada a arrestar al candidato opositor Arturo Araujo. Las catorce familias es un referente de la oligarquía que controló la mayoría de las tierras y la riqueza en El Salvador durante los siglos 19 y 20, incluidos los apellidos de Sola, Llach, Hill, Duenas, Dalton Regalado, Quinonez y Salaverría. Después de tomar posesión el candidato oficial, Araujo y el General Juan Amaya intentaron una Revolución transfronteriza con el aparente apoyo del gobierno de Honduras, entraron a El Salvador con trescientos colaboradores. El ejército Salvadoreño los derrotó tras una dura batalla, y ellos tuvieron que replegarse en Honduras.

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

The **Bryan–Chamorro Treaty** was signed between [Nicaragua](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua "Nicaragua") and the [United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States "United States") on August 5, 1914. It gave the United States full rights over any future [canal built through Nicaragua](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua_Canal "Nicaragua Canal"). The [Wilson administration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presidency_of_Woodrow_Wilson "Presidency of Woodrow Wilson") changed the treaty by adding a provision similar in language to that of the [Platt Amendment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Platt_Amendment "Platt Amendment"), which would have authorized [military intervention in Nicaragua](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_occupation_of_Nicaragua "United States occupation of Nicaragua"). The [United States Senate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Senate "United States Senate") opposed the new provision; in response, it was dropped, and the treaty was formally ratified on June 19, 1916. Eventually, the United States recognized that the canal was unlikely, and at the request of Nicaragua in 1970, the two nations officially abolished the treaty and all its provisions.

The reform-minded president [José Santos Zelaya López](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jos%C3%A9_Santos_Zelaya "José Santos Zelaya") (elected as a [Liberal Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democratic_Party_/(Nicaragua/) "Democratic Party (Nicaragua)") candidate) had incurred the wrath of the United States by negotiating with [France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/France "France"), [Germany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Germany "Germany"), and [Japan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japan "Japan") to resurrect the proposed [Nicaragua Canal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua_Canal "Nicaragua Canal"), which might constitute potential future foreign competition with the newly built, U.S.-owned [Panama Canal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Panama_Canal "Panama Canal"). The United States then supported an insurgency against the government led by Conservative Party insurgents [Emiliano Chamorro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emiliano_Chamorro "Emiliano Chamorro") and [Juan José Estrada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Juan_Jos%C3%A9_Estrada "Juan José Estrada"), supplying them with arms, funds, troops, warships, and also imposing economic measures. This eventually forced the popular liberal Presidents José Zelaya and then [Jose Madriz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jose_Madriz "Jose Madriz") to flee the country. The US then installed the conservative governments of first Juan José Estrada (soon deposed by the powerful Secretary of War [Luis Mena](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luis_Mena_/(Nicaraguan_politician/) "Luis Mena (Nicaraguan politician)")) and then former Vice President [Adolfo Díaz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adolfo_D%C3%ADaz "Adolfo Díaz").

When General Luis Mena convinced the [National Assembly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Assembly "National Assembly") to name him successor to the unpopular pro-U.S. Adolfo Díaz, the United States invaded and occupied Nicaragua militarily from 1912 to 1933, wrote a new constitution for the country, changed the National Assembly, and propped up successive conservative regimes under the presidents Adolfo Díaz, Emiliano Chamorro, and [Diego Manuel Chamorro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diego_Manuel_Chamorro_Bola%C3%B1os "Diego Manuel Chamorro Bolaños"). Luis Mena fled into the countryside to start a rebellion, which continued under various leaders for the next sixty years. In exchange for [political concessions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Concession_/(contract/) "Concession (contract)") from Adolfo Díaz, the United States provided the military strength to suppress popular revolt and ensure the conservative regime maintained control over the Nicaraguan government. For much of the 20th century, Nicaragua remained controlled under the hereditary dictatorship of the Chamorro. After 1936, the Somoza dynasties were controlled until widespread rebellions forced them out of power in the 1970s.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bryan%E2%80%93Chamorro_Treaty#cite_note-Brief-1): 111, 197 [\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bryan%E2%80%93Chamorro_Treaty#cite_note-2)[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bryan%E2%80%93Chamorro_Treaty#cite_note-3)[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bryan%E2%80%93Chamorro_Treaty#cite_note-Musicant-4): 143

The Treaty was named after the principal negotiators: [William Jennings Bryan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Jennings_Bryan "William Jennings Bryan"), U.S. Secretary of State, and the then [General Emiliano Chamorro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emiliano_Chamorro_Vargas "Emiliano Chamorro Vargas"), representing the Nicaraguan government. By the terms of the treaty, the United States acquired the rights to any canal built in Nicaragua in perpetuity, a renewable 99 year option to establish a naval base in the [Gulf of Fonseca](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gulf_of_Fonseca "Gulf of Fonseca"), and a renewable 99-year lease to the Great and Little [Corn Islands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corn_Islands "Corn Islands") in the [Caribbean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caribbean "Caribbean"). Nicaragua received $3 million for those concessions.

Most of the $3 million was paid back to U.S. creditors by U.S. officials in charge of Nicaraguan financial affairs, which allowed the Nicaraguan government to continue to collect internal revenue. The debt had been quickly amassed in a two-year period by the Nicaraguan government of [Juan José Estrada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Juan_Jos%C3%A9_Estrada "Juan José Estrada") under the American ["dollars for bullets"](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dollar_Diplomacy "Dollar Diplomacy") scheme to retard infrastructure development funding from rival powers and lingering debts from earlier indemnities Nicaragua was forced to pay the foreign occupying powers of the United States and [Great Britain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua_Crisis_of_1895#British_occupation_of_Corinto "Nicaragua Crisis of 1895"), and repairing the devastation inflicted from the [war with Great Britain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua_Crisis_of_1895 "Nicaragua Crisis of 1895"), [war with the United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_occupation_of_Nicaragua#Estrada's_rebellion_\(1909\) "United States occupation of Nicaragua") and the [civil war of Luis Mena's Rebellion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_occupation_of_Nicaragua#Mena's_rebellion_\(1912\) "United States occupation of Nicaragua").[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bryan%E2%80%93Chamorro_Treaty#cite_note-Musicant-4): 143 [\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bryan%E2%80%93Chamorro_Treaty#cite_note-5)[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bryan%E2%80%93Chamorro_Treaty#cite_note-6)[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bryan%E2%80%93Chamorro_Treaty#cite_note-7)[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bryan%E2%80%93Chamorro_Treaty#cite_note-8)

The provision of the Bryan–Chamorro Treaty granting rights to the United States to build a naval base in the Gulf of Fonseca was contested by [El Salvador](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Salvador "El Salvador") and [Costa Rica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Costa_Rica "Costa Rica"). The [Central American Court of Justice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_American_Integration_System#First_Central_American_Court_of_Justice "Central American Integration System") favored the two countries.[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bryan%E2%80%93Chamorro_Treaty#cite_note-9) The United States ignored the decision, contributing significantly to the court's collapse in 1918.

Later, the United States recognized that a canal in Nicaragua parallel to the Panama Canal was increasingly unlikely.[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bryan%E2%80%93Chamorro_Treaty#cite_note-Goodsell-10)

[![Image 1](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/38/Tacho_%26_Hope.jpg/250px-Tacho_%26_Hope.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Tacho_%26_Hope.jpg)

Abrogation of the Bryan-Chamorro Treaty, July 14, 1970, in Managua. Nicaraguan President Anastasio Somoza Debayle during a public ceremony held in the lobby of the National Palace, with his wife Hope Portocarrero and ministers of his government.

In 1970, at the request of Nicaragua, the United States under [Richard Nixon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Nixon "Richard Nixon") and Nicaragua under [Anastasio Somoza Debayle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anastasio_Somoza_Debayle "Anastasio Somoza Debayle") held a convention that officially abolished the treaty and all its provisions.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bryan%E2%80%93Chamorro_Treaty#cite_note-11)[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bryan%E2%80%93Chamorro_Treaty#cite_note-Goodsell-10)

At various times since the [Panama Canal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Panama_Canal "Panama Canal") opened in 1914, [the Nicaragua route has been reconsidered](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_Nicaraguan_Canal "History of the Nicaraguan Canal"). Its construction would shorten the water distance between [New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City "New York City") and [San Francisco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Francisco "San Francisco") by nearly 800 kilometers (500 mi). The Bryan–Chamorro Treaty kept Nicaragua from—and stopped any potential European powers from—competing with the Panama Canal.

**Jorge Meléndez Ramírez** (15 April 1871 – 22 November 1953) was a Salvadoran politician and businessman who served as [President of El Salvador](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_El_Salvador "President of El Salvador") from 1919 to 1923. The presidency was the only political office Meléndez ever held. He was the younger brother of President [Carlos Meléndez](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carlos_Mel%C3%A9ndez_/(politician/) "Carlos Meléndez (politician)").

Meléndez became the [1919 presidential candidate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1919_Salvadoran_presidential_election "1919 Salvadoran presidential election") for the [National Democratic Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Democratic_Party_/(El_Salvador/) "National Democratic Party (El Salvador)") (PND) after Carlos resigned as President and the election's frontrunners, [Alfonso Quiñónez Molina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfonso_Qui%C3%B1%C3%B3nez_Molina "Alfonso Quiñónez Molina") and Tomás Palomo, dropped out. Meléndez won the election with almost 97 percent of the vote and assumed office on 1 March 1919. During his presidency, the PND centralized power and monopolized local [patronage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patronage "Patronage") networks. Meléndez suppressed several coups against his rule. He was succeeded in 1923 by Quiñónez, who had served as his [vice president](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_President_of_El_Salvador "Vice President of El Salvador"). Meléndez's presidency was a part of the broader [Meléndez–Quiñónez dynasty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mel%C3%A9ndez%E2%80%93Qui%C3%B1%C3%B3nez_dynasty "Meléndez–Quiñónez dynasty") that ruled El Salvador from 1913 to 1927. Meléndez tried to overthrow President [Pío Romero Bosque](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P%C3%ADo_Romero_Bosque "Pío Romero Bosque") in 1927 as he attempted to curb the dynasty's influence, but the [coup failed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1927_Salvadoran_coup_attempt "1927 Salvadoran coup attempt") and Meléndez left El Salvador for exile in Costa Rica.

Jorge Meléndez Ramírez was born on 15 April 1871 in [San Salvador](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Salvador "San Salvador"), El Salvador. His parents were Rafael Meléndez, a [tailor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tailor "Tailor"), and Mercedes Ramírez. Meléndez was one of nine children.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jorge_Mel%C3%A9ndez#cite_note-FOOTNOTELeistenschneiderLeistenschneider1980175-1)[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jorge_Mel%C3%A9ndez#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEstrada2025-2) Through Meléndez's mother, he was a grandson of [Norberto Ramírez](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norberto_Ram%C3%ADrez "Norberto Ramírez"), the [president of El Salvador](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_El_Salvador "President of El Salvador") in from 1840 to 1841.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jorge_Mel%C3%A9ndez#cite_note-FOOTNOTELeistenschneiderLeistenschneider1980175-1)

Early political career
----------------------

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Jorge_Mel%C3%A9ndez&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Early political career")\]

On 9 February 1913, Salvadoran president [Manuel Enrique Araujo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manuel_Enrique_Araujo "Manuel Enrique Araujo") was assassinated and Meléndez's older brother [Carlos Meléndez](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carlos_Mel%C3%A9ndez_/(politician/) "Carlos Meléndez (politician)") became the country's [provisional president](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_El_Salvador "President of El Salvador").[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jorge_Mel%C3%A9ndez#cite_note-FOOTNOTELeistenschneiderLeistenschneider1980171-3) At the time, Meléndez was a political novice and had never held public office unlike Carlos who had served on the municipal council of San Salvador and ran for president on several occasions during the 1890s and 1900s.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jorge_Mel%C3%A9ndez#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChing1997237%E2%80%93238-4) Carlos was inaugurated as president on 1 March 1915; [Alfonso Quiñónez Molina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfonso_Qui%C3%B1%C3%B3nez_Molina "Alfonso Quiñónez Molina"), his and Meléndez's brother-in-law through Quiñónez's marriage to their sister Leonor, was [Vice President](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_President_of_El_Salvador "Vice President of El Salvador").[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jorge_Mel%C3%A9ndez#cite_note-FOOTNOTELeistenschneiderLeistenschneider1980171-3) Carlos' presidency began a period in Salvadoran history known as the [Meléndez–Quiñónez dynasty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mel%C3%A9ndez%E2%80%93Qui%C3%B1%C3%B3nez_dynasty "Meléndez–Quiñónez dynasty").[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jorge_Mel%C3%A9ndez#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChing19972-5)[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jorge_Mel%C3%A9ndez#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBernal_Ram%C3%ADrezQuijano_de_Batres200955_&_106-6)

> "Why would capitalists risk their money by investing it in a transport business, for example, when in the morning, General X, _jefe_ of a revolutionary band, expropriates it? Why would they put their money into useful enterprises when just as quickly it is extracted by an exaggerated tribute decreed by some irresponsible government born in the clamor of gunfire? \[...\] It is necessary that politics be guided along a path that little by little dispenses with the gangrene of [personalism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Personalism "Personalism"), the primordial cause of our instability."

Jorge Meléndez in _Economic Orientations of President Meléndez_, 14 September 1917[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jorge_Mel%C3%A9ndez#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChing1997243-7)

Meléndez supported Carlos' presidency. In 1917, Meléndez wrote a pamphlet titled _Economic Orientations of President Meléndez_ praising Carlos' presidency as a victory of "civilized society" over _[caudillismo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caudillo "Caudillo")_. He argued that Carlos' centralization of power was preferable to the factionalized violence and military uprisings that were common in 19th century Salvadoran politics.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jorge_Mel%C3%A9ndez#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChing1997243%E2%80%93244-8)

### 1919 presidential campaign

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Jorge_Mel%C3%A9ndez&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: 1919 presidential campaign")\]

Ahead of the [1919 presidential election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1919_Salvadoran_presidential_election "1919 Salvadoran presidential election"), Quiñónez and Minister of Governance and Finance Tomás García Palomo were the election's frontrunners.[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jorge_Mel%C3%A9ndez#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChing1997244-9) On 21 December 1918, Carlos resigned as President as he suffered a [paralytic attack](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paralysis "Paralysis") ten days prior and Quiñónez succeeded him as provisional president. Now that Quiñónez was provisional president, he was constitutionally prohibited from running in the election as he was in the office six months prior to the next presidential term. Palomo also dropped out of the race as he did not want to run against the incumbent president.[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jorge_Mel%C3%A9ndez#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChing1997248%E2%80%93249-10)

In January 1919, one week before the election, Quiñónez selected Meléndez to replace him as the presidential candidate for the [National Democratic Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Democratic_Party_/(El_Salvador/) "National Democratic Party (El Salvador)") (PND),[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jorge_Mel%C3%A9ndez#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChing1997249-11) the party Quiñónez established to initially get himself elected before he became ineligible.[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jorge_Mel%C3%A9ndez#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChing1997246-12) Landowner [Arturo Araujo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arturo_Araujo "Arturo Araujo") of the [Salvadoran Laborist Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salvadoran_Laborist_Party "Salvadoran Laborist Party") announced that he would challenge Meléndez's campaign.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jorge_Mel%C3%A9ndez#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChing1997249-11) In response, Meléndez and Quiñónez ordered [Pío Romero Bosque](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P%C3%ADo_Romero_Bosque "Pío Romero Bosque"), the chief justice of the [Supreme Court of Justice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supreme_Court_of_Justice_of_El_Salvador "Supreme Court of Justice of El Salvador"), to run in the election so that they could humiliate Araujo by making him finish in third place behind Meléndez and Romero. Polling stations were ordered to prevent Araujo's supporters from voting and to also tabulate most votes in favor of Meléndez, the second most in Romero's favor, and allocate whatever was left to Araujo.[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jorge_Mel%C3%A9ndez#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChing1997250%E2%80%93251-13) The final results declared that Meléndez won 166,441 votes (96.86%), Romero won 4,370 votes (2.54%), and Araujo won 1,022 votes (0.59%).[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jorge_Mel%C3%A9ndez#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChing1997251-14)

President of El Salvador
------------------------

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Jorge_Mel%C3%A9ndez&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: President of El Salvador")\]

Meléndez was inaugurated as President of El Salvador on 1 March 1919.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jorge_Mel%C3%A9ndez#cite_note-FOOTNOTELeistenschneiderLeistenschneider1980175-1) Quiñónez was his vice president.[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jorge_Mel%C3%A9ndez#cite_note-FOOTNOTELeistenschneiderLeistenschneider1980179-15) Meléndez's cabinet consisted of [Miguel Tomás Molina](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Miguel_Tom%C3%A1s_Molina&action=edit&redlink=1 "Miguel Tomás Molina (page does not exist)") (a cousin of Quiñónez) as [Minister of Government, Promotion, and Agriculture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ministry_of_the_Interior_/(El_Salvador/) "Ministry of the Interior (El Salvador)"); [José Esperanza Suay](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Jos%C3%A9_Esperanza_Suay&action=edit&redlink=1 "José Esperanza Suay (page does not exist)") as [Minister of Finance and Public Credit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ministry_of_Finance_/(El_Salvador/) "Ministry of Finance (El Salvador)"); [Juan José Paredes](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Juan_Jos%C3%A9_Paredes_\(politician\)&action=edit&redlink=1 "Juan José Paredes (politician) (page does not exist)") as [Minister of External Relations, Public Instruction, Justice, and Charity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_ministers_of_foreign_affairs_of_El_Salvador "List of ministers of foreign affairs of El Salvador"); and Romero as [Minister of War and the Navy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minister_of_National_Defense_/(El_Salvador/) "Minister of National Defense (El Salvador)").[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jorge_Mel%C3%A9ndez#cite_note-FOOTNOTELeistenschneiderLeistenschneider1980175-1) During Meléndez's presidency, the PND centralized power and all political [patronage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patronage "Patronage") networks[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jorge_Mel%C3%A9ndez#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChing1997253-16) and used the [Red League](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Red_League&action=edit&redlink=1 "Red League (page does not exist)") (a paramilitary initially formed by Quiñónez to support his 1919 campaign) to enforce government control.[\[17\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jorge_Mel%C3%A9ndez#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChing1997246%E2%80%93247-17)

### Social and economic policies

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Jorge_Mel%C3%A9ndez&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Social and economic policies")\]

[![Image 3: A black-and-white photograph of Jorge Meléndez surrounded by public workers](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/fc/Jorge_Mel%C3%A9ndez_in_1919.jpg/250px-Jorge_Mel%C3%A9ndez_in_1919.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Jorge_Mel%C3%A9ndez_in_1919.jpg)

Meléndez with public workers in 1919

Meléndez was a pragmatic liberal.[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jorge_Mel%C3%A9ndez#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhite197388-18) Before becoming president, Meléndez promised to allowed trade unions to organize.[\[19\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jorge_Mel%C3%A9ndez#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhite197391-19) This did occur and Meléndez's government actively encouraged urban laborers and artisans to unionize.[\[20\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jorge_Mel%C3%A9ndez#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBernal_Ram%C3%ADrezQuijano_de_Batres200956-20) These unions led to the spread of ideologies such as [socialism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Socialism "Socialism") among Salvadoran workers.[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jorge_Mel%C3%A9ndez#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBernal_Ram%C3%ADrezQuijano_de_Batres200962-21) In 1920, tailors held the first urban strike in Salvadoran history.[\[22\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jorge_Mel%C3%A9ndez#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBernal_Ram%C3%ADrezQuijano_de_Batres200963-22) While unions were allowed to form, Meléndez did not implement wider social reforms.[\[23\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jorge_Mel%C3%A9ndez#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBernal_Ram%C3%ADrezQuijano_de_Batres200957-23) He also only allowed urban unions to form and not rural unions.[\[22\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jorge_Mel%C3%A9ndez#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBernal_Ram%C3%ADrezQuijano_de_Batres200963-22)

During the [Recession of 1920–1921](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Recession_of_1920%E2%80%931921 "Recession of 1920–1921"), Meléndez's government acquired loans from several United States banks that led to an increase in American investments in El Salvador.[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jorge_Mel%C3%A9ndez#cite_note-FOOTNOTELauria-SantiagoGould20086-24)[\[25\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jorge_Mel%C3%A9ndez#cite_note-FOOTNOTEArtiga-Gonz%C3%A1lez201558-25) Meléndez turned a blind eye to [corruption](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corruption_in_El_Salvador "Corruption in El Salvador") and [embezzlement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Embezzlement "Embezzlement") during his presidency.[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jorge_Mel%C3%A9ndez#cite_note-FOOTNOTELindo2016-26)

In 1919, Meléndez suspended wages of the [Salvadoran Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salvadoran_Army "Salvadoran Army") and the [National Guard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Guard_/(El_Salvador/) "National Guard (El Salvador)") to address the [Recession of 1920–1921](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Recession_of_1920%E2%80%931921 "Recession of 1920–1921") after end of [World War I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_I "World War I").[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jorge_Mel%C3%A9ndez#cite_note-FOOTNOTELauria-SantiagoGould20086-24)[\[27\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jorge_Mel%C3%A9ndez#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChing1997260-27) Throughout Meléndez's presidency, army pay was frequently suspended, and when it was paid, it was not paid in full.[\[28\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jorge_Mel%C3%A9ndez#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChing1997261-28) The army also accused Meléndez of allocating army duties to the National Guard and making the gendarmerie more important than the army.[\[27\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jorge_Mel%C3%A9ndez#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChing1997260-27) In 1920, Meléndez proposed implementing reforms that would make the military accountable to civilian courts. Although he never went through with this proposal, the announcement strained government–military relations.[\[29\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jorge_Mel%C3%A9ndez#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChing1997261%E2%80%93262-29)

In March 1920, the Salvadoran government discovered a plot by Araujo to overthrow Meléndez, and subsequently, government forces clashed with Araujo's supporters at Araujo's El Sunza hacienda while attempting to arrest Araujo. Araujo fled El Salvador to [Honduras](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Honduras "Honduras"), and in May 1920, he led an army of around 300 to 1,000 militiamen across the [El Salvador–Honduras border](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Salvador%E2%80%93Honduras_border "El Salvador–Honduras border"). He captured the city of [Arcatao](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arcatao "Arcatao"), but Meléndez's soldiers forced Araujo back across the border. Araujo remained in exile until 1923.[\[30\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jorge_Mel%C3%A9ndez#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChing1997251%E2%80%93252-30) At the same time as Araujo's invasion, two army barracks mutinied but both were suppressed.[\[31\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jorge_Mel%C3%A9ndez#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChing1997262%E2%80%93263-31)

In February 1922, 63 cadets of the Polytechnic School attempted to overthrow Meléndez. They attacked loyalist soldiers in San Salvador resulting in around 50 casualties. The government suppressed the coup within one day and Meléndez shut down the Polytechnic School for four years. Another coup attempt occurred on 22 May 1922 when 200 soldiers of the 6th Infantry Barracks revolted and declared Oliverio Cromwell Valle, an exiled opponent of Meléndez, as president. They attempted to capture the [El Zapote](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Military_Museum_of_the_Armed_Forces_of_El_Salvador "Military Museum of the Armed Forces of El Salvador") barracks but failed.[\[32\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jorge_Mel%C3%A9ndez#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChing1997263%E2%80%93264-32)

### Central America union

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Jorge_Mel%C3%A9ndez&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Central America union")\]

El Salvador briefly joined the [Federation of Central America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federation_of_Central_America_/(1921%E2%80%931922/) "Federation of Central America (1921–1922)") consisting of El Salvador, [Guatemala](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guatemala "Guatemala"), and Honduras.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jorge_Mel%C3%A9ndez#cite_note-FOOTNOTELeistenschneiderLeistenschneider1980175-1) In January 1921, El Salvador sent a delegation to [San José, Costa Rica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Jos%C3%A9,_Costa_Rica "San José, Costa Rica") to negotiate the establishment of a [new Central American union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_American_reunification "Central American reunification"). They drafted the Pact of Union of Central America,[\[33\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jorge_Mel%C3%A9ndez#cite_note-FOOTNOTETipograf%C3%ADa_Nacional19213%E2%80%934-33) and on 9 September 1921, El Salvador ratified the Central American constitution.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jorge_Mel%C3%A9ndez#cite_note-FOOTNOTELeistenschneiderLeistenschneider1980175-1) The union collapsed in December 1921 after a coup d'état in Guatemala.[\[34\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jorge_Mel%C3%A9ndez#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPerry192248-34)

Post-presidency and death
-------------------------

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Jorge_Mel%C3%A9ndez&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Post-presidency and death")\]

[![Image 4: A black-and-white photograph of people running through an urban street](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/53/Christmas_Day_Massacre_%28El_Salvador%29.jpg/250px-Christmas_Day_Massacre_%28El_Salvador%29.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Christmas_Day_Massacre_/(El_Salvador/).jpg)

Rally attendants fleeing the scene of the [Christmas Day Massacre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christmas_Day_Massacre_/(El_Salvador/) "Christmas Day Massacre (El Salvador)") perpetrated by Meléndez's [Red League](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Red_League&action=edit&redlink=1 "Red League (page does not exist)") paramilitary

Meléndez left office on 1 March 1923 and was succeeded by Quiñónez who unanimously won the [1923 presidential election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1923_Salvadoran_presidential_election "1923 Salvadoran presidential election").[\[35\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jorge_Mel%C3%A9ndez#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChing1997280-35)[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jorge_Mel%C3%A9ndez#cite_note-FOOTNOTELeistenschneiderLeistenschneider1980179-15) His victory came after Meléndez banned political rallies and the Red League [massacred dozens of Molina's supporters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christmas_Day_Massacre_/(El_Salvador/) "Christmas Day Massacre (El Salvador)") (who challenged Quiñónez) at a political rally on 25 December 1922.[\[36\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jorge_Mel%C3%A9ndez#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChing1997277%E2%80%93278-36) According to [Montgomery Schuyler Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montgomery_Schuyler_Jr. "Montgomery Schuyler Jr."), the [United States ambassador to El Salvador](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_United_States_ambassadors_to_El_Salvador&action=edit&redlink=1 "List of United States ambassadors to El Salvador (page does not exist)"), Meléndez offered a toast to the massacre in 1923.[\[35\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jorge_Mel%C3%A9ndez#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChing1997280-35) Meléndez never held public office after leaving the presidency.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jorge_Mel%C3%A9ndez#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChing1997237%E2%80%93238-4)

In 1927, Quiñónez was succeeded as president by Romero.[\[37\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jorge_Mel%C3%A9ndez#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChing1997286-37) Quiñónez intended to continue ruling through Romero who would serve as a [puppet ruler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Puppet_ruler "Puppet ruler"),[\[38\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jorge_Mel%C3%A9ndez#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhite197394%E2%80%9395-38) but Romero sought to distance himself from the dynasty and forced several of Quiñónez's government officials to resign.[\[39\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jorge_Mel%C3%A9ndez#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChing1997305-39) He also lifted press censorship leading to protests against Quiñónez's occupation of the office of [First Presidential Designate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_El_Salvador#Succession "President of El Salvador") (second in line to the presidency after the vice president). Quiñónez left the country for exile in France, but he and Meléndez plotted a coup to overthrow Romero and preserve the dynasty's political influence.[\[40\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jorge_Mel%C3%A9ndez#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChing1997306%E2%80%93308-40)

Meléndez, the coup's primary organizer, recruited several allies to execute the coup and raised an army of 500 militiamen at his Valencia hacienda.[\[41\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jorge_Mel%C3%A9ndez#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChing1997309-41) On 7 December 1927, Colonel Juan Enrique Aberle and Major Manuel Alfaro Noguera (participants of the coup) told Chief of Police Colonel Enrique Leitzelar that a [military junta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Military_junta "Military junta") proclaimed Aberle as the country's president, but Leitzelar demanded confirmation from General Carlos Carmona Tadey, the commander of the 1st Infantry Regiment. Carmona was supposed to be involved in the coup but denied any knowledge of such a junta existing. Aberle and Noguera surrendered but later told Romero that he had been overthrown and offered him safe passage out of El Salvador. Romero had Aberle and Noguera arrested and the coup collapsed. Meléndez never mobilized his militiamen and subsequently fled the country to Costa Rica after the [United States embassy in San Salvador](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Embassy_of_the_United_States,_San_Salvador "Embassy of the United States, San Salvador") denied his asylum request.[\[42\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jorge_Mel%C3%A9ndez#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChing1997310%E2%80%93311-42)[\[43\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jorge_Mel%C3%A9ndez#cite_note-FOOTNOTECastellanos200158-43) In Costa Rica, Meléndez invested in the sugar industry.[\[44\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jorge_Mel%C3%A9ndez#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChing1997311-44)

Meléndez died in San Salvador on 22 November 1953.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jorge_Mel%C3%A9ndez#cite_note-FOOTNOTELeistenschneiderLeistenschneider1980175-1)

[![Image 5: A black-and-white photograph of the Venecia sugar hacienda](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/66/%22Venecia%22_sugar_hacienda_in_El_Salvador_%284%29.png/250px-%22Venecia%22_sugar_hacienda_in_El_Salvador_%284%29.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:%22Venecia%22_sugar_hacienda_in_El_Salvador_/(4/).png)

The Venecia sugar [hacienda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hacienda "Hacienda") owned by Meléndez[\[45\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jorge_Mel%C3%A9ndez#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWard1916222-45)

Meléndez married Tula Mazzini and the couple had 3 children: Jorge, María de los Ángeles, and Ricardo.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jorge_Mel%C3%A9ndez#cite_note-FOOTNOTELeistenschneiderLeistenschneider1980175-1)

Meléndez was an agriculturalist. He owned at least three [haciendas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hacienda "Hacienda") named Prusia, Valencia, and Venecia; some raised cattle and others produced sugar.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jorge_Mel%C3%A9ndez#cite_note-FOOTNOTELeistenschneiderLeistenschneider1980175-1)[\[45\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jorge_Mel%C3%A9ndez#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWard1916222-45)[\[46\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jorge_Mel%C3%A9ndez#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChing1997238_&_310-46) Meléndez and Carlos were El Salvador's largest sugar producers during the Meléndez–Quiñónez dynasty. According to a 1929 agricultural census, Meléndez owned over half of the land in the city of [Soyapango](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soyapango "Soyapango").[\[47\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jorge_Mel%C3%A9ndez#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChing1997238-47) Meléndez also owned shares of the Central American Insurance Company and the Artesian Well Drilling Company of Salvador.[\[45\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jorge_Mel%C3%A9ndez#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWard1916222-45) American agronomist Frederick William Taylor described Meléndez as a "very wealthy man with all sorts of activities going on".[\[48\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jorge_Mel%C3%A9ndez#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChing1997239-48)
