**Alfonso Quiñónez Molina** (Latin American Spanish: [\[alˈfonso kiˈɲones moˈlina\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/Spanish "Help:IPA/Spanish"); 11 January 1874 – 22 May 1950) was a Salvadoran politician and physician who served as [President of El Salvador](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_El_Salvador "President of El Salvador") on three occasions during the 1910s and 1920s. Between his presidencies, he also served as [Vice President of El Salvador](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_President_of_El_Salvador "Vice President of El Salvador") on two occasions under his brothers-in-law [Carlos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carlos_Mel%C3%A9ndez_/(politician/) "Carlos Meléndez (politician)") and [Jorge Meléndez](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jorge_Mel%C3%A9ndez "Jorge Meléndez"). The presidencies of Quiñónez and his brothers-in-law from 1913 to 1927 are collectively known as the [Meléndez–Quiñónez dynasty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mel%C3%A9ndez%E2%80%93Qui%C3%B1%C3%B3nez_dynasty "Meléndez–Quiñónez dynasty").[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfonso_Qui%C3%B1%C3%B3nez_Molina#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBernal_Ram%C3%ADrezQuijano_de_Batres2009106-1)

Alfonso Quiñónez Molina was born on 11 January 1874 in [Suchitoto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suchitoto "Suchitoto"), El Salvador.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfonso_Qui%C3%B1%C3%B3nez_Molina#cite_note-FOOTNOTELeistenschneiderLeistenschneider1980179-2)[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfonso_Qui%C3%B1%C3%B3nez_Molina#cite_note-FOOTNOTECa%C3%B1as_DinarteScarlett_Cortez200657-3)[\[a\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfonso_Qui%C3%B1%C3%B3nez_Molina#cite_note-5) His parents were Lucio Quiñónez and Aurelia Molina de Quiñónez. Quiñónez studied medicine at the Liceo San Luis in [Santa Tecla](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santa_Tecla,_El_Salvador "Santa Tecla, El Salvador"). He then studied at the [University of El Salvador](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_El_Salvador "University of El Salvador") and earned his [Doctorate of Medicine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doctorate_of_Medicine "Doctorate of Medicine") in surgery in 1898. Quiñónez practiced medicine at the General Hospital of [San Salvador](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Salvador "San Salvador") beginning in 1897,[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfonso_Qui%C3%B1%C3%B3nez_Molina#cite_note-FOOTNOTECa%C3%B1as_DinarteScarlett_Cortez200657-3) and the following year, he was became a member of the board of the country's insane asylum. He also served as the chair of the hygiene and therapeutics and a counselor of the medical faculty at the University of El Salvador. In 1904, Quiñónez became the director of the insane asylum, and in 1906, he was an acting physician for the country's [Red Cross](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Red_Cross_and_Red_Crescent_Movement "International Red Cross and Red Crescent Movement") society.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfonso_Qui%C3%B1%C3%B3nez_Molina#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWard1916148-6)

Quiñónez married Leonor Meléndez in 1905.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfonso_Qui%C3%B1%C3%B3nez_Molina#cite_note-FOOTNOTELeistenschneiderLeistenschneider1980179-2) Two of Quiñónez's brothers-in-law through his marriage to Leonor Meléndez were [Carlos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carlos_Mel%C3%A9ndez_/(politician/) "Carlos Meléndez (politician)") and [Jorge Meléndez](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jorge_Mel%C3%A9ndez "Jorge Meléndez").[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfonso_Qui%C3%B1%C3%B3nez_Molina#cite_note-FOOTNOTECa%C3%B1as_DinarteScarlett_Cortez200657%E2%80%9358-7)

Early political career
----------------------

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Alfonso_Qui%C3%B1%C3%B3nez_Molina&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Early political career")\]

Quiñónez was a pragmatic liberal.[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfonso_Qui%C3%B1%C3%B3nez_Molina#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhite197388-8) In 1903, Quiñónez was elected as an alderman of the San Salvador city council.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfonso_Qui%C3%B1%C3%B3nez_Molina#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWard1916148%E2%80%93149-9) In 1912, he was elected as the [mayor of San Salvador](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayor_of_San_Salvador "Mayor of San Salvador")[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfonso_Qui%C3%B1%C3%B3nez_Molina#cite_note-FOOTNOTECa%C3%B1as_DinarteScarlett_Cortez200658-10) and as an alternate deputy of the [Legislative Assembly of El Salvador](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Legislative_Assembly_of_El_Salvador "Legislative Assembly of El Salvador").[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfonso_Qui%C3%B1%C3%B3nez_Molina#cite_note-FOOTNOTECa%C3%B1as_DinarteScarlett_Cortez200653-11)

Presidencies and vice presidencies
----------------------------------

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Alfonso_Qui%C3%B1%C3%B3nez_Molina&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Presidencies and vice presidencies")\]

### First presidency and vice presidency

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Alfonso_Qui%C3%B1%C3%B3nez_Molina&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: First presidency and vice presidency")\]

On 9 February 1913, Quiñónez's brother-in-law Carlos Meléndez became the provisional [president of El Salvador](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_El_Salvador "President of El Salvador") upon the assassination of President [Manuel Enrique Araujo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manuel_Enrique_Araujo "Manuel Enrique Araujo"). Carlos Meléndez succeeded Araujo as he was the country's [first presidential designate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_El_Salvador#Succession "President of El Salvador") and Vice President [Onofre Durán Santillana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Onofre_Dur%C3%A1n_Santillana "Onofre Durán Santillana") had earlier resigned.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfonso_Qui%C3%B1%C3%B3nez_Molina#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChing1997220-12)[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfonso_Qui%C3%B1%C3%B3nez_Molina#cite_note-FOOTNOTELeistenschneiderLeistenschneider1980171-13) On 4 March 1914, the Legislative Assembly named Quiñónez as the first presidential designate,[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfonso_Qui%C3%B1%C3%B3nez_Molina#cite_note-FOOTNOTECa%C3%B1as_DinarteScarlett_Cortez200658-10) and on 21 December 1914, Quiñónez became the country's provisional president upon Carlos Meléndez's resignation in order to [run for president in 1915](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1915_Salvadoran_presidential_election "1915 Salvadoran presidential election").[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfonso_Qui%C3%B1%C3%B3nez_Molina#cite_note-FOOTNOTELeistenschneiderLeistenschneider1980180-14)[\[b\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfonso_Qui%C3%B1%C3%B3nez_Molina#cite_note-16)

Quiñónez's cabinet consisted of [Francisco Martínez Suárez](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Francisco_Mart%C3%ADnez_Su%C3%A1rez&action=edit&redlink=1 "Francisco Martínez Suárez (page does not exist)") as [minister of exterior relations, public instruction, and justice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_ministers_of_foreign_affairs_of_El_Salvador "List of ministers of foreign affairs of El Salvador"); [Cecilio Bustamante](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Cecilio_Bustamante&action=edit&redlink=1 "Cecilio Bustamante (page does not exist)") as [minister of government, promotion, and agriculture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ministry_of_the_Interior_/(El_Salvador/) "Ministry of the Interior (El Salvador)"); [Samuel Luna](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Samuel_Luna&action=edit&redlink=1 "Samuel Luna (page does not exist)") as [minister of finance, public credit, and benefits](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ministry_of_Finance_/(El_Salvador/) "Ministry of Finance (El Salvador)"); and [Pío Romero Bosque](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P%C3%ADo_Romero_Bosque "Pío Romero Bosque") as [minister of war and the navy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minister_of_National_Defense_/(El_Salvador/) "Minister of National Defense (El Salvador)").[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfonso_Qui%C3%B1%C3%B3nez_Molina#cite_note-FOOTNOTELeistenschneiderLeistenschneider1980180-14) During Quiñónez's first provisional presidency, he established the Military Hospital.[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfonso_Qui%C3%B1%C3%B3nez_Molina#cite_note-FOOTNOTELeistenschneiderLeistenschneider1980181-17)

Carlos Meléndez won the 1915 presidential election[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfonso_Qui%C3%B1%C3%B3nez_Molina#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChing1997237-18) and appointed Quiñónez to serve as [vice president](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_President_of_El_Salvador "Vice President of El Salvador").[\[17\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfonso_Qui%C3%B1%C3%B3nez_Molina#cite_note-FOOTNOTELeistenschneiderLeistenschneider1980172-19)

### Second presidency and vice presidency

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Alfonso_Qui%C3%B1%C3%B3nez_Molina&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Second presidency and vice presidency")\]

On 21 December 1918, Carlos Meléndez resigned as president due to illness, and Quiñónez assumed the presidency in a provisional capacity.[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfonso_Qui%C3%B1%C3%B3nez_Molina#cite_note-FOOTNOTELeistenschneiderLeistenschneider1980181-17) Quiñónez's second cabinet consisted of Bustamante as minister of government, promotion, and agriculture and [Enrique Córdova](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Enrique_C%C3%B3rdova&action=edit&redlink=1 "Enrique Córdova (page does not exist)") as minister of war and the navy.[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfonso_Qui%C3%B1%C3%B3nez_Molina#cite_note-FOOTNOTELeistenschneiderLeistenschneider1980180-14)

In 1918, Quiñónez established the Lega Rojas, or the Red league, which intended to work as a mediator between the oligarchy and the peasants. It was deemed as the first attempt to form an official party in the country. However, the far-reaching oligarchic control of the prevented the organization from achieving its goal. Later it supported the candidacy of President Jorge Meléndez.\[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_\]

[![Image 2: A black-and-white photograph of several men standing and facing the camera](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b6/Miembros_del_Gabinete_y_Ejercito_del_Gobierno_del_Dr._Alfonso_Qui%C3%B1onez_Molina_%E2%80%93_1926.jpg/250px-Miembros_del_Gabinete_y_Ejercito_del_Gobierno_del_Dr._Alfonso_Qui%C3%B1onez_Molina_%E2%80%93_1926.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Miembros_del_Gabinete_y_Ejercito_del_Gobierno_del_Dr._Alfonso_Qui%C3%B1onez_Molina_%E2%80%93_1926.jpg)

Quiñónez with members of his third cabinet in 1926

Quiñónez won the [1923 presidential election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1923_Salvadoran_presidential_election "1923 Salvadoran presidential election") unanimously with 176,000 votes.[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfonso_Qui%C3%B1%C3%B3nez_Molina#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChing1997280-20) He was inaugurated on 1 March 1923 and his cabinet consisted of [Francisco Lima](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Francisco_Lima_\(politician\)&action=edit&redlink=1 "Francisco Lima (politician) (page does not exist)") as minister of government, promotion, and agriculture; [Reyes Arrieta Rossi](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Reyes_Arrieta_Rossi&action=edit&redlink=1 "Reyes Arrieta Rossi (page does not exist)") as minister of exterior relations, public instruction, and justice; [Calixto Velado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Calixto_Velado "Calixto Velado") as minister of finance, public credit, and benefits; and Romero as minister of war and the navy. Romero also served as Quiñónez's vice president.[\[19\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfonso_Qui%C3%B1%C3%B3nez_Molina#cite_note-FOOTNOTELeistenschneiderLeistenschneider1980180%E2%80%93181-21)

As president, Quiñónez invested in the construction of railways and highways.[\[20\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfonso_Qui%C3%B1%C3%B3nez_Molina#cite_note-FOOTNOTEConsulate_General_of_El_Salvador19257-22)

Quiñónez handed the presidency to Vice President [Pío Romero Bosque](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P%C3%ADo_Romero_Bosque "Pío Romero Bosque"). He thought that as Romero did not spring from a rich family, he would be a puppet.

Later life and death
--------------------

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Alfonso_Qui%C3%B1%C3%B3nez_Molina&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Later life and death")\]

Quiñónez, along with other members of the dynasty organized a coup against Romero. However, the coup, which took place in December 1927, ultimately failed. After this, Romero exiled Quiñónez from El Salvador.[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfonso_Qui%C3%B1%C3%B3nez_Molina#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHaggerty199014-23) Quiñónez returned to El Salvador in 1936.[\[22\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfonso_Qui%C3%B1%C3%B3nez_Molina#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMart%C3%ADnez_Pe%C3%B1ateS%C3%A1nchez2004442-24)

Quiñónez died on 22 May 1950 in San Salvador.[\[23\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfonso_Qui%C3%B1%C3%B3nez_Molina#cite_note-FOOTNOTELeistenschneiderLeistenschneider1980182-25)

[![Image 1: This is a good article. Click here for more information.](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/9/94/Symbol_support_vote.svg/20px-Symbol_support_vote.svg.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Good_articles* "This is a good article. Click here for more information.")

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

The **Meléndez–Quiñónez dynasty** ([Spanish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_language "Spanish language"): _dinastía Meléndez-Quiñónez_) was a period in [El Salvador](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Salvador "El Salvador")'s history from 1913 to 1927 when the Salvadoran government was controlled by the Meléndez–Quiñónez [political family](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Political_family "Political family").[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mel%C3%A9ndez%E2%80%93Qui%C3%B1%C3%B3nez_dynasty#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChing19972-1)[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mel%C3%A9ndez%E2%80%93Qui%C3%B1%C3%B3nez_dynasty#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBernal_Ram%C3%ADrezQuijano_de_Batres200956-2)[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mel%C3%A9ndez%E2%80%93Qui%C3%B1%C3%B3nez_dynasty#cite_note-FOOTNOTECastellanos200152-3) During this period, three of the family's members—brothers [Carlos Meléndez](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carlos_Mel%C3%A9ndez_/(politician/) "Carlos Meléndez (politician)") and [Jorge Meléndez](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jorge_Mel%C3%A9ndez "Jorge Meléndez") and their brother-in-law [Alfonso Quiñónez Molina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfonso_Qui%C3%B1%C3%B3nez_Molina "Alfonso Quiñónez Molina")—rotated control of the [presidency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_El_Salvador "President of El Salvador") between themselves.

The dynasty began in 1913 when Carlos became president after [Manuel Enrique Araujo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manuel_Enrique_Araujo "Manuel Enrique Araujo")'s assassination. Carlos resigned in 1914 to run in the [1915 presidential election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1915_Salvadoran_presidential_election "1915 Salvadoran presidential election") and was briefly succeeded by Quiñónez. Carlos won the election and served until his resignation in 1918. Quiñónez again succeeded him, and Carlos' younger brother Jorge won the [1919 election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1919_Salvadoran_presidential_election "1919 Salvadoran presidential election"). He served until 1923 when he was succeeded by Quiñónez. Quiñónez served until 1927 when he was succeeded by [Pío Romero Bosque](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P%C3%ADo_Romero_Bosque "Pío Romero Bosque"), his [minister of war](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minister_of_National_Defense_/(El_Salvador/) "Minister of National Defense (El Salvador)") and a personal friend. Quiñónez intended to continue ruling El Salvador through Romero as a [puppet ruler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Puppet_ruler "Puppet ruler"), but Romero politically broke from the Meléndez–Quiñónez dynasty. Jorge and Quiñónez attempted to overthrow Romero, but their December 1927 coup attempt failed, ending the dynasty's influence in El Salvador.

The Meléndez–Quiñónez dynasty ruled El Salvador in an [authoritarian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Authoritarianism "Authoritarianism") manner.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mel%C3%A9ndez%E2%80%93Qui%C3%B1%C3%B3nez_dynasty#cite_note-FOOTNOTELauria-SantiagoGould200832-4) It utilized [fraudulent elections](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electoral_fraud "Electoral fraud") and [political repression](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Political_repression "Political repression") by the [Red League](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Red_League&action=edit&redlink=1 "Red League (page does not exist)") [paramilitary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paramilitary "Paramilitary") to hold onto power. Jorge and Quiñónez established the [National Democratic Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Democratic_Party_/(El_Salvador/) "National Democratic Party (El Salvador)") (PDN) in 1918 to ensure that its allies got elected to political offices. In 1922, the Red League killed a dozen people who supported a rival in the [1923 presidential election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1923_Salvadoran_presidential_election "1923 Salvadoran presidential election") during the [Christmas Day Massacre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christmas_Day_Massacre_/(El_Salvador/) "Christmas Day Massacre (El Salvador)"). The dynasty benefitted economically from high coffee prices and foreign investments; meanwhile, Salvadoran workers protested and demanded more rights and improved working conditions.

[![Image 2: A black-and-white portrait of Manuel Enrique Araujo](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/98/Manuel_Enrique_Araujo_01.jpg/250px-Manuel_Enrique_Araujo_01.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Manuel_Enrique_Araujo_01.jpg)

[Manuel Enrique Araujo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manuel_Enrique_Araujo "Manuel Enrique Araujo"), whose assassination led to the rise of the Meléndez–Quiñónez dynasty

On 9 February 1913, Salvadoran president [Manuel Enrique Araujo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manuel_Enrique_Araujo "Manuel Enrique Araujo") died from wounds sustained in an assassination attempt five days prior.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mel%C3%A9ndez%E2%80%93Qui%C3%B1%C3%B3nez_dynasty#cite_note-FOOTNOTETrabanino1999-5)[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mel%C3%A9ndez%E2%80%93Qui%C3%B1%C3%B3nez_dynasty#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKuny_Mena2003-6) As Vice President [Onofre Durán Santillana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Onofre_Dur%C3%A1n_Santillana "Onofre Durán Santillana") resigned before Manuel Enrique Araujo's death, [Carlos Meléndez](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carlos_Mel%C3%A9ndez_/(politician/) "Carlos Meléndez (politician)"), the [president of the Legislative Assembly of El Salvador](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_presidents_of_the_Legislative_Assembly_of_El_Salvador "List of presidents of the Legislative Assembly of El Salvador") and the [first presidential designate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_El_Salvador#Succession "President of El Salvador"), succeeded Manuel Enrique Araujo as the provisional [president](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_El_Salvador "President of El Salvador").[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mel%C3%A9ndez%E2%80%93Qui%C3%B1%C3%B3nez_dynasty#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChing1997220-7)[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mel%C3%A9ndez%E2%80%93Qui%C3%B1%C3%B3nez_dynasty#cite_note-FOOTNOTELeistenschneiderLeistenschneider1980171-8) Shortly after assuming office, Carlos had Manuel Enrique Araujo's assassins [executed by firing squad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Executed_by_firing_squad "Executed by firing squad").[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mel%C3%A9ndez%E2%80%93Qui%C3%B1%C3%B3nez_dynasty#cite_note-FOOTNOTELeistenschneiderLeistenschneider1980172-9)

Carlos had been active in Salvadoran politics since the 1894 [Revolution of the 44](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Revolution_of_the_44 "Revolution of the 44") that brought General [Rafael Antonio Gutiérrez](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rafael_Antonio_Guti%C3%A9rrez "Rafael Antonio Gutiérrez") to power.[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mel%C3%A9ndez%E2%80%93Qui%C3%B1%C3%B3nez_dynasty#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChing1997175_&_237-10) Carlos ran for [vice president](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_President_of_El_Salvador "Vice President of El Salvador") in the [1895 election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1895_Salvadoran_presidential_election "1895 Salvadoran presidential election") but lost to [Prudencio Alfaro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prudencio_Alfaro "Prudencio Alfaro") by 19,214 votes.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mel%C3%A9ndez%E2%80%93Qui%C3%B1%C3%B3nez_dynasty#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChing1997175-11) Carlos ran for vice president again in the [1903 election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1903_Salvadoran_presidential_election "1903 Salvadoran presidential election"), and for president in 1903 and [1907](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1907_Salvadoran_presidential_election "1907 Salvadoran presidential election"), but was unsuccessful each time.[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mel%C3%A9ndez%E2%80%93Qui%C3%B1%C3%B3nez_dynasty#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDiario_Oficial1903298-12)[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mel%C3%A9ndez%E2%80%93Qui%C3%B1%C3%B3nez_dynasty#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDiario_Oficial1907354-13) Carlos intended to be elected to the presidency in the [1915 presidential election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1915_Salvadoran_presidential_election "1915 Salvadoran presidential election") and established the Club Melendista (a pseudo-political party) to help him win the election. The club ensured that only his allies would be elected to local offices so that they could select election officials who would guarantee Carlos' victory.[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mel%C3%A9ndez%E2%80%93Qui%C3%B1%C3%B3nez_dynasty#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChing1997239-14)

On 29 August 1914, Carlos resigned from the presidency and handed it to his brother-in-law [Alfonso Quiñónez Molina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfonso_Qui%C3%B1%C3%B3nez_Molina "Alfonso Quiñónez Molina"), the country's first presidential designate.[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mel%C3%A9ndez%E2%80%93Qui%C3%B1%C3%B3nez_dynasty#cite_note-FOOTNOTELeistenschneiderLeistenschneider1980180-15) Carlos did this because he would have been constitutionally ineligible to run for president in the 1915 presidential election if he did not resign early. The constitution prohibited anyone who had held the office of President in the six months prior to an election from participating in it, as a way to prevent consecutive re-election.[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mel%C3%A9ndez%E2%80%93Qui%C3%B1%C3%B3nez_dynasty#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChing1997242-16) Carlos ultimately won the 1915 election[\[17\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mel%C3%A9ndez%E2%80%93Qui%C3%B1%C3%B3nez_dynasty#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChing1997237-17) and was inaugurated as President on 1 March 1915. Quiñónez became his vice president.[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mel%C3%A9ndez%E2%80%93Qui%C3%B1%C3%B3nez_dynasty#cite_note-FOOTNOTELeistenschneiderLeistenschneider1980171%E2%80%93172-18)

Rule over El Salvador
---------------------

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Mel%C3%A9ndez%E2%80%93Qui%C3%B1%C3%B3nez_dynasty&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Rule over El Salvador")\]

### Centralization of power

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Mel%C3%A9ndez%E2%80%93Qui%C3%B1%C3%B3nez_dynasty&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Centralization of power")\]

[![Image 3: A family tree visualizing the family relations of the Meléndez–Quiñónez dynasty and the political offices its members held](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/9d/Mel%C3%A9ndez%E2%80%93Qui%C3%B1%C3%B3nez_Dynasty_Family_Tree.png/500px-Mel%C3%A9ndez%E2%80%93Qui%C3%B1%C3%B3nez_Dynasty_Family_Tree.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Mel%C3%A9ndez%E2%80%93Qui%C3%B1%C3%B3nez_Dynasty_Family_Tree.png)

Family connections of the Meléndez–Quiñónez dynasty[\[19\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mel%C3%A9ndez%E2%80%93Qui%C3%B1%C3%B3nez_dynasty#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWard191610%E2%80%9311-19)[\[20\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mel%C3%A9ndez%E2%80%93Qui%C3%B1%C3%B3nez_dynasty#cite_note-FOOTNOTELeistenschneiderLeistenschneider198057_&_171%E2%80%93179-20)

Once the Meléndez–Quiñónez dynasty was in power, it sought to ensure that it would remain in power through the use of fraudulent and rigged elections that would favor the dynasty.[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mel%C3%A9ndez%E2%80%93Qui%C3%B1%C3%B3nez_dynasty#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBernal_Ram%C3%ADrezQuijano_de_Batres200955-21) Political scientist Michael Krennerich wrote that El Salvador's elections during the Meléndez–Quiñónez dynasty "had little political significance" outside of a small [oligarchy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oligarchy "Oligarchy") that was allowed to participate.[\[22\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mel%C3%A9ndez%E2%80%93Qui%C3%B1%C3%B3nez_dynasty#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKrennerich2005270-22) Furthermore, those that were allowed to participate in elections all had political positions similar to those of the dynasty. According to historians Luis Guillermo Bernal Ramírez and Ana Elia Quijano de Batres, "the entire country" ("_todo el país_") knew that elections were fraudulent.[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mel%C3%A9ndez%E2%80%93Qui%C3%B1%C3%B3nez_dynasty#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBernal_Ram%C3%ADrezQuijano_de_Batres200955-21) One contemporary election official remarked that "presidential continuance depend\[ed\] often enough on electoral fraud".[\[23\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mel%C3%A9ndez%E2%80%93Qui%C3%B1%C3%B3nez_dynasty#cite_note-FOOTNOTELauria-SantiagoGould200834-23)

> "Why would capitalists risk their money by investing it in a transport business, for example, when in the morning, General X, _jefe_ of a revolutionary band, expropriates it? Why would they put their money into useful enterprises when just as quickly it is extracted by an exaggerated tribute decreed by some irresponsible government born in the clamor of gunfire? \[...\] It is necessary that politics be guided along a path that little by little dispenses with the gangrene of [personalism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Personalism "Personalism"), the primordial cause of our instability."

[Jorge Meléndez](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jorge_Mel%C3%A9ndez "Jorge Meléndez") in _Economic Orientations of President Meléndez_, 14 September 1917[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mel%C3%A9ndez%E2%80%93Qui%C3%B1%C3%B3nez_dynasty#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChing1997243-24)

In mid-1918, [Jorge Meléndez](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jorge_Mel%C3%A9ndez "Jorge Meléndez") (Carlos' younger brother) and Quiñónez established the [National Democratic Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Democratic_Party_/(El_Salvador/) "National Democratic Party (El Salvador)") (PND) to consolidate their political networks and allegiances. All political activity outside the party was soon outlawed.[\[25\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mel%C3%A9ndez%E2%80%93Qui%C3%B1%C3%B3nez_dynasty#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChing1997214_&_246-25) During Carlos' presidency, the Meléndez brothers portrayed their government and a break from the country's past of factionalized violence and revolutions. In a pamphlet titled _Economic Orientations of President Meléndez_, Jorge praised his brother's presidency as having defeated _[caudillismo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caudillo "Caudillo")_ in the name of "civilized government". They presented this liberal and democratic portrayal of the government to justify their centralization of power into their government, the Club Melendista, and the PND.[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mel%C3%A9ndez%E2%80%93Qui%C3%B1%C3%B3nez_dynasty#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChing1997243%E2%80%93244-26) The PND had a [paramilitary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paramilitary "Paramilitary") wing known as the [Red League](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Red_League&action=edit&redlink=1 "Red League (page does not exist)") ("_Liga Roja_") that intimidated opponents with violence.[\[27\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mel%C3%A9ndez%E2%80%93Qui%C3%B1%C3%B3nez_dynasty#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChing1997246%E2%80%93247-27)[\[28\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mel%C3%A9ndez%E2%80%93Qui%C3%B1%C3%B3nez_dynasty#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBernal_Ram%C3%ADrezQuijano_de_Batres200957%E2%80%9359-28) Many of the Red League's members were clients of the dynasty's allies and Indigenous Salvadorans that sought to use the paramilitary's training for their own political advantage.[\[29\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mel%C3%A9ndez%E2%80%93Qui%C3%B1%C3%B3nez_dynasty#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChing1997247_&_258-29)

In the lead up to the [1919 presidential election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1919_Salvadoran_presidential_election "1919 Salvadoran presidential election"), Carlos did not designate a presidential successor, so Quiñónez and Tomás García Palomo (Carlos' minister of government and finance) ran against each other.[\[30\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mel%C3%A9ndez%E2%80%93Qui%C3%B1%C3%B3nez_dynasty#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChing1997244-30) During the December 1918 municipal elections, Quiñónez and Palomo's supporters clashed with each other at polling stations, killing around 100 people and wounding 200 more. The election resulted in Quiñónez's allies winning, virtually assuring him victory in the presidential election.[\[31\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mel%C3%A9ndez%E2%80%93Qui%C3%B1%C3%B3nez_dynasty#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChing1997247%E2%80%93248-31) On 21 December 1918, Carlos resigned as president due to illness and Quiñónez assumed the presidency, disqualifying him from participating in the election. Quiñónez considered running anyway, and Palomo subsequently dropped out of the race because he did not want to run against the incumbent president.[\[32\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mel%C3%A9ndez%E2%80%93Qui%C3%B1%C3%B3nez_dynasty#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChing1997248%E2%80%93249-32) One week before the election, Quiñónez selected Jorge to be the PND's candidate.[\[33\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mel%C3%A9ndez%E2%80%93Qui%C3%B1%C3%B3nez_dynasty#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChing1997249-33) Landowner [Arturo Araujo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arturo_Araujo "Arturo Araujo") (no relation to Manuel Enrique Araujo)[\[34\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mel%C3%A9ndez%E2%80%93Qui%C3%B1%C3%B3nez_dynasty#cite_note-FOOTNOTECastellanos200154-34) of the [Salvadoran Laborist Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salvadoran_Laborist_Party "Salvadoran Laborist Party") also announced his own campaign. In response, Jorge and Quiñónez ordered [Supreme Court](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supreme_Court_of_Justice_of_El_Salvador "Supreme Court of Justice of El Salvador") Chief Justice [Pío Romero Bosque](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P%C3%ADo_Romero_Bosque "Pío Romero Bosque") to run and they planned to have him receive more votes than Arturo Araujo to humiliate him. The election resulted in Jorge receiving 97 percent of the vote, Romero receiving 2 percent, and Arturo Araujo receiving 1 percent.[\[35\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mel%C3%A9ndez%E2%80%93Qui%C3%B1%C3%B3nez_dynasty#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChing1997249%E2%80%93251-35)

### Violence and rebellions

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Mel%C3%A9ndez%E2%80%93Qui%C3%B1%C3%B3nez_dynasty&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Violence and rebellions")\]

Jorge was inaugurated as president of El Salvador on 1 March 1919.[\[36\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mel%C3%A9ndez%E2%80%93Qui%C3%B1%C3%B3nez_dynasty#cite_note-FOOTNOTELeistenschneiderLeistenschneider1980175-36) Carlos died on 8 October 1919 in [New York City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City "New York City"), United States due to complications from the same illness that had led to his resignation.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mel%C3%A9ndez%E2%80%93Qui%C3%B1%C3%B3nez_dynasty#cite_note-FOOTNOTELeistenschneiderLeistenschneider1980171-8) In 1920, Arturo Araujo attempted to seize power by invading El Salvador from Honduras with an army of 300 to 1,000 militiamen, but Jorge's government repelled the invasion.[\[37\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mel%C3%A9ndez%E2%80%93Qui%C3%B1%C3%B3nez_dynasty#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChing1997251%E2%80%93252-37) During Jorge's presidency, he and Quiñónez expanded the PND's influence, and many of the party's local officials labeled [independent politicians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Independent_politician "Independent politician") and non-PND members as enemies.[\[38\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mel%C3%A9ndez%E2%80%93Qui%C3%B1%C3%B3nez_dynasty#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChing1997253-38) The government also used the [military](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Armed_Forces_of_El_Salvador "Armed Forces of El Salvador") to ensure that PND candidates won local elections and prevent factionalism.[\[39\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mel%C3%A9ndez%E2%80%93Qui%C3%B1%C3%B3nez_dynasty#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChing1997256%E2%80%93257-39)

Government–military relations began to deteriorate during Jorge's presidency, especially as the government cut [army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salvadoran_Army "Salvadoran Army") wages in 1919 due to budget deficits. The military was also dissatisfied with the treatment of the [National Guard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Guard_/(El_Salvador/) "National Guard (El Salvador)") (a [gendarmerie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gendarmerie "Gendarmerie")) which it saw as supplanting it in importance.[\[40\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mel%C3%A9ndez%E2%80%93Qui%C3%B1%C3%B3nez_dynasty#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChing1997260-40) In February 1922, 63 cadets of the Polytechnic School attempted a [coup d'état](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coup_d%27%C3%A9tat "Coup d'état") against Jorge's government and killed around 50 loyalist soldiers. The coup failed and Jorge closed the school for four years. In May 1922, 200 soldiers of the 6th Infantry Brigade in [San Salvador](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Salvador "San Salvador") took control of their barracks and declared Jorge to be deposed. The rebelling soldiers failed to capture the [El Zapote barracks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Military_Museum_of_the_Armed_Forces_of_El_Salvador "Military Museum of the Armed Forces of El Salvador"); 40 were captured or killed while the remaining soldiers fled the country.[\[41\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mel%C3%A9ndez%E2%80%93Qui%C3%B1%C3%B3nez_dynasty#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChing1997263%E2%80%93264-41)

[![Image 4: A black-and-white photograph of several men standing and facing the camera](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b6/Miembros_del_Gabinete_y_Ejercito_del_Gobierno_del_Dr._Alfonso_Qui%C3%B1onez_Molina_%E2%80%93_1926.jpg/250px-Miembros_del_Gabinete_y_Ejercito_del_Gobierno_del_Dr._Alfonso_Qui%C3%B1onez_Molina_%E2%80%93_1926.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Miembros_del_Gabinete_y_Ejercito_del_Gobierno_del_Dr._Alfonso_Qui%C3%B1onez_Molina_%E2%80%93_1926.jpg)

[Alfonso Quiñónez Molina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfonso_Qui%C3%B1%C3%B3nez_Molina "Alfonso Quiñónez Molina") with members of his cabinet in 1926

Quiñónez was the PND's candidate in the [1923 presidential election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1923_Salvadoran_presidential_election "1923 Salvadoran presidential election"). [Miguel Tomás Molina](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Miguel_Tom%C3%A1s_Molina&action=edit&redlink=1 "Miguel Tomás Molina (page does not exist)"), Jorge's former minister of government and one of Quiñónez's cousins, challenged Quiñónez's presidential bid.[\[42\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mel%C3%A9ndez%E2%80%93Qui%C3%B1%C3%B3nez_dynasty#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChing1997266_&_275-42) Jorge implemented a [state of emergency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/State_of_emergency "State of emergency") that prevented Molina from holding political rallies to support his campaign.[\[43\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mel%C3%A9ndez%E2%80%93Qui%C3%B1%C3%B3nez_dynasty#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChing1997277-43) Despite the ban on rallies, Molina held a rally on 25 December 1922 in downtown San Salvador. The Red League, National Guard, [National Police](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Police_of_El_Salvador "National Police of El Salvador"), and army shot at people attending the rally, killing around a dozen people and injuring around a hundred.[\[44\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mel%C3%A9ndez%E2%80%93Qui%C3%B1%C3%B3nez_dynasty#cite_note-FOOTNOTELauria-SantiagoGould200839-44) Molina sought refuge in the Spanish embassy after the [Christmas Day Massacre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christmas_Day_Massacre_/(El_Salvador/) "Christmas Day Massacre (El Salvador)"),[\[45\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mel%C3%A9ndez%E2%80%93Qui%C3%B1%C3%B3nez_dynasty#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChing1997278-45)[\[46\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mel%C3%A9ndez%E2%80%93Qui%C3%B1%C3%B3nez_dynasty#cite_note-FOOTNOTECa%C3%B1as_Dinarte2022-46) and on election day, Quiñónez won unanimously with 178,000 votes.[\[47\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mel%C3%A9ndez%E2%80%93Qui%C3%B1%C3%B3nez_dynasty#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChing1997280-47) Romero was elected as his vice president, and they both assumed office on 1 March 1923.[\[48\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mel%C3%A9ndez%E2%80%93Qui%C3%B1%C3%B3nez_dynasty#cite_note-FOOTNOTELeistenschneiderLeistenschneider1980179-48) Quiñónez disbanded the Red League in 1923 after assuming the presidency because it began to engage in politics outside of his orders.[\[49\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mel%C3%A9ndez%E2%80%93Qui%C3%B1%C3%B3nez_dynasty#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChing1997272-49)

Fall of the dynasty
-------------------

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Mel%C3%A9ndez%E2%80%93Qui%C3%B1%C3%B3nez_dynasty&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Fall of the dynasty")\]

### Conflict with Romero

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Mel%C3%A9ndez%E2%80%93Qui%C3%B1%C3%B3nez_dynasty&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Conflict with Romero")\]

[![Image 5: A black-and-white portrait photograph of Pío Romero Bosque](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/79/Dr_Pio_Romero_Bosque%2C_pr%C3%A9sident_de_Salvador_%28Pacific%29_-_btv1b532073706_%28cropped%29.jpg/250px-Dr_Pio_Romero_Bosque%2C_pr%C3%A9sident_de_Salvador_%28Pacific%29_-_btv1b532073706_%28cropped%29.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Dr_Pio_Romero_Bosque,_pr%C3%A9sident_de_Salvador_/(Pacific/)_-_btv1b532073706_/(cropped/).jpg)

[Pío Romero Bosque](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P%C3%ADo_Romero_Bosque "Pío Romero Bosque"), Quiñónez's vice president and successor who ended the dynasty

As the [1927 presidential election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1927_Salvadoran_presidential_election "1927 Salvadoran presidential election") approached, Quiñónez nominated Romero as his presidential successor. Romero agreed to retain certain political appointments made by Quiñónez as a precondition for Quiñónez picking him as the next president.[\[50\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mel%C3%A9ndez%E2%80%93Qui%C3%B1%C3%B3nez_dynasty#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChing1997305-50) Romero won the election unanimously and assumed office on 1 March 1927.[\[51\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mel%C3%A9ndez%E2%80%93Qui%C3%B1%C3%B3nez_dynasty#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChing1997286-51)[\[52\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mel%C3%A9ndez%E2%80%93Qui%C3%B1%C3%B3nez_dynasty#cite_note-FOOTNOTECortez_Tejada2023139-52) Quiñónez expected to use Romero as a [puppet ruler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Puppet_ruler "Puppet ruler"),[\[53\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mel%C3%A9ndez%E2%80%93Qui%C3%B1%C3%B3nez_dynasty#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhite197395-53)[\[54\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mel%C3%A9ndez%E2%80%93Qui%C3%B1%C3%B3nez_dynasty#cite_note-FOOTNOTELauria-SantiagoGould200841-54) and contemporary American diplomats such as [Cornelius Van Hemert Engert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cornelius_Van_Hemert_Engert "Cornelius Van Hemert Engert") and [Jefferson Caffery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jefferson_Caffery "Jefferson Caffery") also believed that Quiñónez would continue to [rule El Salvador behind the scenes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Power_behind_the_throne "Power behind the throne").[\[55\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mel%C3%A9ndez%E2%80%93Qui%C3%B1%C3%B3nez_dynasty#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChing1997290-55)[\[56\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mel%C3%A9ndez%E2%80%93Qui%C3%B1%C3%B3nez_dynasty#cite_note-FOOTNOTEvan_den_Berk2016231-56) In 1927, the Legislative Assembly appointed Quiñónez as the first presidential designee, second in line to the presidency after Vice President [Gustavo Vides](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gustavo_Vides "Gustavo Vides").[\[50\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mel%C3%A9ndez%E2%80%93Qui%C3%B1%C3%B3nez_dynasty#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChing1997305-50)

In April 1927, Romero backtracked on his agreement with Quiñónez to maintain existing political appointments by forcing two of his sub-secretaries to resign, which led to Quiñónez accusing him of failing to uphold his political promises. Engert believed that the forced resignations were part of a campaign by Romero to "do away with the Quinonez \[_[sic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sic "Sic")_\] influence".[\[50\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mel%C3%A9ndez%E2%80%93Qui%C3%B1%C3%B3nez_dynasty#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChing1997305-50) That same month, Romero also lifted press censorship and the ban on public demonstrations and, soon after, [University of El Salvador](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_El_Salvador "University of El Salvador") students protested in San Salvador against Quiñónez's appointment as the first presidential designate, even protesting in front of his home demanding his resignation. In June 1927, as Quiñónez's and Romero's supporters in the Legislative Assembly debated the constitutionality of Quiñónez's appointment, Quiñónez resigned and left with his family for exile in France.[\[57\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mel%C3%A9ndez%E2%80%93Qui%C3%B1%C3%B3nez_dynasty#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChing1997306%E2%80%93307-57)

### 1927 pro-dynasty coup attempt

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Mel%C3%A9ndez%E2%80%93Qui%C3%B1%C3%B3nez_dynasty&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: 1927 pro-dynasty coup attempt")\]

Jorge and Quiñónez plotted a coup to overthrow Romero's government to preserve the dynasty's influence in Salvadoran politics.[\[58\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mel%C3%A9ndez%E2%80%93Qui%C3%B1%C3%B3nez_dynasty#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChing1997308-58) Jorge was the coup's primary organizer and he recruited several of his and Quiñónez's allies to carry it out. Among those recruited to the plot were Federico Guillermo Kreitz (chief of police under the Meléndez–Quiñónez dynasty), Colonel Juan Enrique Aberle (the incumbent chief of the army's machine shop), and Major Manuel Alfaro Noguera (the incumbent deputy chief of police). Jorge and Kreitz recruited around 500 militiamen armed with machetes.[\[59\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mel%C3%A9ndez%E2%80%93Qui%C3%B1%C3%B3nez_dynasty#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChing1997309-59)[\[60\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mel%C3%A9ndez%E2%80%93Qui%C3%B1%C3%B3nez_dynasty#cite_note-FOOTNOTECastellanos200158-60)

On 6 December 1927, Aberle and Noguera arrived at the country's police headquarters and told Chief of Police Colonel Enrique Leitzelar that an unspecified [military junta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Military_junta "Military junta") had proclaimed Aberle as the country's president and Noguera as the new chief of police. Leitzelar demanded confirmation of this information from General [Carlos Carmona Tadey](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Carlos_Carmona_Tadey&action=edit&redlink=1 "Carlos Carmona Tadey (page does not exist)"), the commander of the 1st Infantry Regiment; Carmona (who was supposed to be a coup collaborator) denied any knowledge of Aberle and Noguera's proclamation. Both Aberle and Noguera then surrendered. When they were both brought before Romero himself, Aberle told Romero the same news that he had told Leitzelar and offered him and his family safe passage out of El Salvador if he resigned peacefully. Romero instead had Aberle and Noguera arrested, and had them both court martialed and executed by firing squad two days later. The 500 militiamen did not participate in the coup attempt, and Jorge subsequently fled the country to Honduras and later Costa Rica after being denied asylum by the [United States embassy in El Salvador](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Embassy_of_the_United_States,_San_Salvador "Embassy of the United States, San Salvador").[\[60\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mel%C3%A9ndez%E2%80%93Qui%C3%B1%C3%B3nez_dynasty#cite_note-FOOTNOTECastellanos200158-60)[\[61\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mel%C3%A9ndez%E2%80%93Qui%C3%B1%C3%B3nez_dynasty#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChing1997310%E2%80%93311-61)

In a February 1928 interview with [Montgomery Schuyler Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montgomery_Schuyler_Jr. "Montgomery Schuyler Jr.") (former U.S. [chargé d'affaires](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charg%C3%A9_d%27affaires "Chargé d'affaires") to El Salvador), Quiñónez expressed his sympathy to the coup and condemned the executions of Aberle and Noguera.[\[62\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mel%C3%A9ndez%E2%80%93Qui%C3%B1%C3%B3nez_dynasty#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChing1997311-62) Regarding his relationship with Romero, Quiñónez said:

> "You know, of course, that we are no longer friends with Romero Bosque. We were old friends. He was in my government. I helped him greatly. But we have nothing to do with each other now."[\[62\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mel%C3%A9ndez%E2%80%93Qui%C3%B1%C3%B3nez_dynasty#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChing1997311-62)

The coup's failure ended the Meléndez–Quiñónez dynasty's influence in El Salvador.[\[63\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mel%C3%A9ndez%E2%80%93Qui%C3%B1%C3%B3nez_dynasty#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChing1997311%E2%80%93312-63) Romero went on to implement democratic reforms in El Salvador and allow for greater political participation. On 6 September 1927, Romero dissolved the National Democratic Party and banned politicians from running for election under its banner.[\[64\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mel%C3%A9ndez%E2%80%93Qui%C3%B1%C3%B3nez_dynasty#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChing1997314-64) While some candidates with no former ties to the PND were elected in 1927 and 1929 municipal elections, many politicians elected during the Meléndez–Quiñónez dynasty stayed in power.[\[65\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mel%C3%A9ndez%E2%80%93Qui%C3%B1%C3%B3nez_dynasty#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChing1997323%E2%80%93324_&_346-65) In the [1928 legislative election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1928_Salvadoran_legislative_election "1928 Salvadoran legislative election"), Romero pre-selected a set of candidates that would ensure his political allies were elected.[\[a\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mel%C3%A9ndez%E2%80%93Qui%C3%B1%C3%B3nez_dynasty#cite_note-67) Historian Erik Ching theorized that Romero did not extend his democratic reforms to the legislative election as he did not want to allow his enemies to potentially impeach him.[\[66\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mel%C3%A9ndez%E2%80%93Qui%C3%B1%C3%B3nez_dynasty#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChing1997340-66) [Alberto Gómez Zárate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alberto_G%C3%B3mez_Z%C3%A1rate "Alberto Gómez Zárate") (Romero's [minister of war, the navy, and aviation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minister_of_National_Defense_/(El_Salvador/) "Minister of National Defense (El Salvador)")) ran in the [1931 presidential election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1931_Salvadoran_presidential_election "1931 Salvadoran presidential election"). Many saw him as being closely associated with the Meléndez–Quiñónez dynasty, and many former members of the PND supported his campaign.[\[67\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mel%C3%A9ndez%E2%80%93Qui%C3%B1%C3%B3nez_dynasty#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChing1997351-68) Ultimately, Arturo Araujo won the election,[\[68\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mel%C3%A9ndez%E2%80%93Qui%C3%B1%C3%B3nez_dynasty#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChing1997354-69) but he was [overthrown by the military](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1931_Salvadoran_coup_d%27%C3%A9tat "1931 Salvadoran coup d'état") later that year, which ushered in [five decades of military rule](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Military_dictatorship_in_El_Salvador "Military dictatorship in El Salvador").[\[69\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mel%C3%A9ndez%E2%80%93Qui%C3%B1%C3%B3nez_dynasty#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChing1997356_&_363%E2%80%93364-70)

Politics and policies
---------------------

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Mel%C3%A9ndez%E2%80%93Qui%C3%B1%C3%B3nez_dynasty&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Politics and policies")\]

The Meléndez brothers and Quiñónez were all pragmatic [liberals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liberalism "Liberalism").[\[70\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mel%C3%A9ndez%E2%80%93Qui%C3%B1%C3%B3nez_dynasty#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhite197388-71) Supporters and allies of the Meléndez–Quiñónez dynasty were known as _melendistas_[\[71\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mel%C3%A9ndez%E2%80%93Qui%C3%B1%C3%B3nez_dynasty#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChing199775-72) or _quiñonistas_.[\[72\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mel%C3%A9ndez%E2%80%93Qui%C3%B1%C3%B3nez_dynasty#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBernal_Ram%C3%ADrezQuijano_de_Batres200958-73) The dynasty's supporters included Indigenous Salvadorans, to whom the dynasty promised the restoration of land,[\[73\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mel%C3%A9ndez%E2%80%93Qui%C3%B1%C3%B3nez_dynasty#cite_note-FOOTNOTELauria-SantiagoGould200835-74) and the country's wealthy landowners who benefited from the dynasty's economic policies.[\[74\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mel%C3%A9ndez%E2%80%93Qui%C3%B1%C3%B3nez_dynasty#cite_note-FOOTNOTELauria-SantiagoGould200836%E2%80%9337-75)

[![Image 6: A black-and-white photograph of Jorge Meléndez surrounded by public workers](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/fc/Jorge_Mel%C3%A9ndez_in_1919.jpg/250px-Jorge_Mel%C3%A9ndez_in_1919.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Jorge_Mel%C3%A9ndez_in_1919.jpg)

[Jorge Meléndez](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jorge_Mel%C3%A9ndez "Jorge Meléndez") with public workers in 1919

[![Image 7: A black-and-white photograph of coffee plantation workers waiting in line to receive their wages](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/5f/Arbetare_p%C3%A5_en_kaffeplantage_i_El_Salvador_1927_SLSA_1232-3_foto_14.jpg/250px-Arbetare_p%C3%A5_en_kaffeplantage_i_El_Salvador_1927_SLSA_1232-3_foto_14.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Arbetare_p%C3%A5_en_kaffeplantage_i_El_Salvador_1927_SLSA_1232-3_foto_14.jpg)

Salvadoran coffee plantation workers waiting in line to receive their wages in 1927

During the Meléndez–Quiñónez dynasty, the Salvadoran economy was heavily reliant on [coffee exports](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coffee_production_in_El_Salvador "Coffee production in El Salvador").[\[75\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mel%C3%A9ndez%E2%80%93Qui%C3%B1%C3%B3nez_dynasty#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhite197399-76) When the price of coffee exports fell during the [Recession of 1920–1921](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Recession_of_1920%E2%80%931921 "Recession of 1920–1921"), the Salvadoran government acquired loans from banks in the United States.[\[76\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mel%C3%A9ndez%E2%80%93Qui%C3%B1%C3%B3nez_dynasty#cite_note-FOOTNOTELauria-SantiagoGould20086-77) These loans and subsequent spending led to an increase in American investments in El Salvador, and some Americans even immigrated to El Salvador and gained a controlling stake in El Salvador's coffee production.[\[77\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mel%C3%A9ndez%E2%80%93Qui%C3%B1%C3%B3nez_dynasty#cite_note-FOOTNOTEArtiga-Gonz%C3%A1lez201558-78) By 1926, El Salvador has doubled its pre-[World War I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_I "World War I") coffee production and exported 110,000,000 pounds (50,000,000 kg) of coffee that year, becoming the leading coffee producer in Central America.[\[76\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mel%C3%A9ndez%E2%80%93Qui%C3%B1%C3%B3nez_dynasty#cite_note-FOOTNOTELauria-SantiagoGould20086-77) This, together with record-high coffee prices up to [SV₡](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salvadoran_col%C3%B3n "Salvadoran colón")32 per 100 pounds (45 kg) by 1927, led the country's economy to grow substantially.[\[75\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mel%C3%A9ndez%E2%80%93Qui%C3%B1%C3%B3nez_dynasty#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhite197399-76) While coffee was El Salvador's main export, Salvadoran government officials and American immigrant merchants also sought to diversify El Salvador's economy by investing in cotton and sugar production.[\[78\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mel%C3%A9ndez%E2%80%93Qui%C3%B1%C3%B3nez_dynasty#cite_note-FOOTNOTEArtiga-Gonz%C3%A1lez201558%E2%80%9359-79)[\[79\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mel%C3%A9ndez%E2%80%93Qui%C3%B1%C3%B3nez_dynasty#cite_note-FOOTNOTELauria-SantiagoGould20087%E2%80%938-80) [Corruption](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corruption_in_El_Salvador "Corruption in El Salvador"), [embezzlement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Embezzlement "Embezzlement"), and [extortion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Extortion "Extortion") were common during the Meléndez–Quiñónez dynasty.[\[80\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mel%C3%A9ndez%E2%80%93Qui%C3%B1%C3%B3nez_dynasty#cite_note-FOOTNOTELindo2016-81)

The Meléndez–Quiñónez dynasty did not implement social reform programs, but it did allow and encourage urban laborers and artisans to organize and form unions.[\[81\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mel%C3%A9ndez%E2%80%93Qui%C3%B1%C3%B3nez_dynasty#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBernal_Ram%C3%ADrezQuijano_de_Batres200956%E2%80%9358_&_63-82) This led to the spread of ideologies such as [socialism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Socialism "Socialism") and [communism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Communism "Communism") among Salvadoran workers. While some urban workers' rights progressed, the government continued to protect the interests of the country's wealthy landowners through the National Guard and did not allow rural workers' living conditions to improve.[\[82\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mel%C3%A9ndez%E2%80%93Qui%C3%B1%C3%B3nez_dynasty#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBernal_Ram%C3%ADrezQuijano_de_Batres200957_&_63-83) In 1920, urban tailors held the first recorded strike in Salvadoran history to protest abuse from their employers.[\[83\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mel%C3%A9ndez%E2%80%93Qui%C3%B1%C3%B3nez_dynasty#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBernal_Ram%C3%ADrezQuijano_de_Batres200963-84) Other groups such as teachers, railroad workers, and bakers, among others, also held strikes throughout 1920 and 1921. [Anarcho-syndicalist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anarcho-syndicalism "Anarcho-syndicalism") groups such as the [Regional Federation of the Workers of El Salvador](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Regional_Federation_of_the_Workers_of_El_Salvador&action=edit&redlink=1 "Regional Federation of the Workers of El Salvador (page does not exist)") (FRTS) emerged during the 1920s and demanded land redistribution, an eight-hour workday, and literacy programs from the Meléndez–Quiñónez government.[\[84\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mel%C3%A9ndez%E2%80%93Qui%C3%B1%C3%B3nez_dynasty#cite_note-FOOTNOTEArtiga-Gonz%C3%A1lez201563-85)

Carlos opposed the [Bryan–Chamorro Treaty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bryan%E2%80%93Chamorro_Treaty "Bryan–Chamorro Treaty") between Nicaragua and the United States as it appeared to infringe on Nicaragua's sovereignty and opened the possibility of a U.S. naval base being built in the [Gulf of Fonseca](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gulf_of_Fonseca "Gulf of Fonseca").[\[85\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mel%C3%A9ndez%E2%80%93Qui%C3%B1%C3%B3nez_dynasty#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHolden200464-86) Carlos promoted the "Meléndez Doctrine" ("_Doctrina Meléndez_") that declared the [Gulf of Fonseca](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gulf_of_Fonseca "Gulf of Fonseca") as a "territorial bay" ("_bahía territorial_"), recognizing it as a [condominium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Condominium_/(international_law/) "Condominium (international law)") shared by El Salvador, Honduras, and Nicaragua instead of it being divided by the three countries.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mel%C3%A9ndez%E2%80%93Qui%C3%B1%C3%B3nez_dynasty#cite_note-FOOTNOTECastellanos200152-3)[\[86\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mel%C3%A9ndez%E2%80%93Qui%C3%B1%C3%B3nez_dynasty#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBernal_Ram%C3%ADrezQuijano_de_Batres200974-87) According to Salvadoran diplomat [Rafael Guirola Duke](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Rafael_Guirola_Duke&action=edit&redlink=1 "Rafael Guirola Duke (page does not exist)"), Carlos despised the U.S. and sympathized with the [German Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/German_Empire "German Empire") during [World War I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_I "World War I").[\[85\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mel%C3%A9ndez%E2%80%93Qui%C3%B1%C3%B3nez_dynasty#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHolden200464-86) As such, El Salvador remained neutral during the war and retained its embassies with both the German Empire and [Austria-Hungary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Austria-Hungary "Austria-Hungary").[\[87\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mel%C3%A9ndez%E2%80%93Qui%C3%B1%C3%B3nez_dynasty#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBernal_Ram%C3%ADrezQuijano_de_Batres200935-88)[\[88\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mel%C3%A9ndez%E2%80%93Qui%C3%B1%C3%B3nez_dynasty#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHolden200465-89) Minister of Foreign Relations [José Gustavo Guerrero](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jos%C3%A9_Gustavo_Guerrero "José Gustavo Guerrero") later denounced the doctrine in 1928.[\[60\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mel%C3%A9ndez%E2%80%93Qui%C3%B1%C3%B3nez_dynasty#cite_note-FOOTNOTECastellanos200158-60)

El Salvador briefly joined the short-lived [Federation of Central America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federation_of_Central_America_/(1921%E2%80%931922/) "Federation of Central America (1921–1922)") from 1921 to 1922.[\[89\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mel%C3%A9ndez%E2%80%93Qui%C3%B1%C3%B3nez_dynasty#cite_note-FOOTNOTETipograf%C3%ADa_Nacional19213%E2%80%934-90)[\[90\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mel%C3%A9ndez%E2%80%93Qui%C3%B1%C3%B3nez_dynasty#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPerry192248-91) The federation failed in part due to Nicaragua's inability to join due to the Bryan–Chamorro Treaty[\[91\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mel%C3%A9ndez%E2%80%93Qui%C3%B1%C3%B3nez_dynasty#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPerry192235%E2%80%9336-92) and due to a coup d'état in Guatemala installing a military government that withdrew Guatemala from the federation.[\[92\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mel%C3%A9ndez%E2%80%93Qui%C3%B1%C3%B3nez_dynasty#cite_note-FOOTNOTESanz_y_Tovar1950128%E2%80%93129-93)

[![Image 8: A black-and-white photograph of the Venecia sugar hacienda](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/66/%22Venecia%22_sugar_hacienda_in_El_Salvador_%284%29.png/250px-%22Venecia%22_sugar_hacienda_in_El_Salvador_%284%29.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:%22Venecia%22_sugar_hacienda_in_El_Salvador_/(4/).png)

The Venecia sugar [hacienda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hacienda "Hacienda") owned by Jorge Meléndez[\[93\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mel%C3%A9ndez%E2%80%93Qui%C3%B1%C3%B3nez_dynasty#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWard1916222-94)

Both the Meléndez and Quiñónez families were very wealthy and owned several properties including 16 [haciendas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hacienda "Hacienda") and multiple coffee and sugar plantations. The Meléndez brothers were largest producers of sugar in El Salvador during the time of the Meléndez–Quiñónez dynasty.[\[94\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mel%C3%A9ndez%E2%80%93Qui%C3%B1%C3%B3nez_dynasty#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChing1997238-95) Ching wrote that North American and European visitors to El Salvador during the Meléndez–Quiñónez dynasty "did not miss on the opportunity to comment" on the wealth of Quiñónez and the Meléndez brothers.[\[95\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mel%C3%A9ndez%E2%80%93Qui%C3%B1%C3%B3nez_dynasty#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChing1997238%E2%80%93239-96) Jorge used his wealth to finance the failed December 1927 coup against Romero's government.[\[59\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mel%C3%A9ndez%E2%80%93Qui%C3%B1%C3%B3nez_dynasty#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChing1997309-59) Despite the Meléndez and Quiñónez families' wealth, many Salvadoran oligarchs looked down upon them as they had relatively recently earned their wealth.[\[23\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mel%C3%A9ndez%E2%80%93Qui%C3%B1%C3%B3nez_dynasty#cite_note-FOOTNOTELauria-SantiagoGould200834-23)

The following graph visualizes the timeline of the presidencies of the Meléndez–Quiñónez dynasty, as well as those of Manuel Enrique Araujo (whose assassination led to the dynasty's rise) and Romero (whose policies ended the dynasty's influence). In total, the dynasty ruled El Salvador for 14 years and 20 days from 9 February 1913 to 1 March 1927.

Quiñones Molina, Alfonso (1873–1950)
====================================

Alfonso Quiñones Molina (_b._ 1873; _d._ 1950), president of [El Salvador](https://www.encyclopedia.com/places/latin-america-and-caribbean/salvadoran-political-geography/el-salvador) (1914–1915, 1918–1919, and 1923–1927). Alfonso Quiñones Molina belonged to the Quiñones-Meléndez Family dynasty that controlled the presidency of [El Salvador](https://www.encyclopedia.com/places/latin-america-and-caribbean/salvadoran-political-geography/el-salvador). Members of the dominant civilian landowning elite, these families used rigged elections to maintain governmental control from the 1890s until the [Great Depression](https://www.encyclopedia.com/history/united-states-and-canada/us-history/great-depression) brought military control in 1931. The landowners facilitated the emergence of coffee as the dominant agricultural crop during an era characterized by peace, prosperity, and the concentration of land ownership among a few families.

Quiñones Molina held the presidency three times. He governed briefly in 1914 during the election that installed his brother-in-law, Carlos Meléndez (acting president, 1913–1914). After organizing the first official party, the Liga Roja (Red League) in 1918, he again held office during a transition that allowed the election of Jorge Meléndez (president 1919–1923). Quiñones Molina became president in his own right in 1923, serving until 1927. His controversial foreign borrowing to secure funds for street paving in [San Salvador](https://www.encyclopedia.com/places/latin-america-and-caribbean/salvadoran-political-geography/san-salvador) caused a rejection of external debt by the populace, a situation that was exploited by later military regimes, particularly that of General Maximiliano Hernández Martínez.

_See also_**[El Salvador](https://www.encyclopedia.com/humanities/encyclopedias-almanacs-transcripts-and-maps/el-salvador-0); [Meléndez Family](https://www.encyclopedia.com/humanities/encyclopedias-almanacs-transcripts-and-maps/melendez-family).**

BIBLIOGRAPHY
------------

There are no detailed studies of this era. A laudatory contemporary account can be found in Juan Ramón Uriarte, _La esfinge de Cuzcatlán (el Presidente Quiñones)_ (1929); a brief general discussion in English can be found in Alastair White, _El Salvador_ (1973).

**Liga Roja** . Fue una organización concebida por Alfonso Quiñones Molina, operando en la misma las fuerzas armadas y la guardia nacional como aparatos de dominio en [El Salvador](https://www.ecured.cu/El_Salvador "El Salvador").

Descripción
-----------

Los primeros pasos para la organización popular en El Salvador fue mediante la creación o formación de la Liga Roja en 1917. Los propósitos de esta orgnización popular eran profundamente políticos, aunque se le concideraba en ocasiones como un organismo vinculado a la izquierda revolucionaria.

Esta organización concebida por [Alfonso Quiñones Molina](https://www.ecured.cu/Alfonso_Qui%C3%B1ones_Molina "Alfonso Quiñones Molina") fue un instrumento para manipular a las clases desposeidas en beneficio de los camarillas que se mantenian en el poder.

La Liga Roja tenía como emblema una bandera roja, un programa impregnado de vagos sentimientos socialistas, y una milicia armada propia que operaba con la bendición del gobierno.

Los partidos políticos que operaban en esta liga los nombraban “Los Descamizados” y los miembros de los partidos de oposición se denominaban “Los levudos”, ambos de una u otra forma se vinculaban a la oligarquía terrateniente, bautizándose con el nombre de vanguardias de la clase obrera.

Fuentes
-------

(Suchisoto, 1874 - San Salvador, 1950) Político salvadoreño que fue elegido presidente de la República en 1923 por un período de cuatro años, con lo que continuaba la labor de gobierno de la dinastía Meléndez-Quiñones, que gobernó El Salvador desde 1914 a 1927. Era uno de los principales dirigentes del Partido Demócrata, desde cuyas filas participó numerosas veces en los asuntos políticos del país, donde defendía los intereses de la oligarquía cafetera.

![Image 1](https://www.biografiasyvidas.com/biografia/q/fotos/quinones_molina.jpg)  
Alfonso Quiñones Molina

Durante los mandatos de los presidentes de Carlos Meléndez (1913-1914; 1915-1918), de quien era cuñado, y del hermano de aquél, Jorge Meléndez (1919-1923), ocupó el puesto de vicepresidente, lo cual significaba también hacerse cargo de forma interina de la presidencia del país en 1914 y 1918, hasta que el nuevo presidente tomase posesión.

En 1918, Quiñones fundó la organización conocida con el nombre de la Liga Roja con el objetivo de que actuase como mediador entre el gobierno y los trabajadores, incluidos los campesinos, con lo cual trataba de suplir la falta de sindicatos y partidos políticos. Pero, a pesar de sus intenciones, su pertenencia a la burguesía cafetera no le permitió convertir la liga en una forma mínimamente satisfactoria de representación popular, si bien utilizó la estructura de la Liga Roja para promover la elección de Jorge Meléndez, en lo que se puede considerar como el primer intento en la historia de El Salvador de crear un partido oficialista.

En 1923 fue elegido presidente constitucional de la República de El Salvador por un período de cuatro años. A pesar de que la Constitución proclamaba que el país era una República liberal, actuó como si fuera un dictador que representaba los intereses de las oligárquicas. Impidió en todo momento el funcionamiento de los grupos de oposición. La represión se hizo algo habitual en el país.

Para ganarse el favor popular, en mayo de 1926 decretó la reducción de precio de los alquileres de las viviendas y permitió la creación de corporaciones privadas cuya finalidad era la de construir casas de bajo precio. Cerca de la finalización de su mandato oficial nombró como su sucesor a su paisano, Pío Romero Bosque, quien había sido vicepresidente de su gobierno. La práctica de nombrar a su heredero político era lo habitual entre los presidentes salvadoreños, ya que de esta forma respetaban la Constitución que prohibía la reelección y se aseguraban de poner a alguien favorable a sus intereses al frente del gobierno.

Quiñones cedió la presidencia a su sustituto el 1 de marzo de 1927. Pensaba que, al no ser miembro de una de las grandes familias latifundistas del país, el nuevo presidente sería una marioneta en sus manos. Pero Romero no trabajaba para la familia Meléndez-Quiñones y, desde el primer momento, dio muestras de su independencia. Esto llevó al ex presidente a organizar junto a Jorge Meléndez y otros miembros de la oligarquía salvadoreña un golpe de Estado militar para derrocar al presidente. La acción, que se produjo en diciembre de 1927, acabó en un rotundo fracaso.

![Image 1: Jorge Meléndez, presidente de El Salvador entre 1919 y 1923, rodeado de empleados públicos, en una fotografía tomada en 1919. Foto cortesía Héctor Lindo.](https://elfaro.net/get_img?ImageWidth=1000&ImageHeight=667&ImageId=25623)

Jorge Meléndez, presidente de El Salvador entre 1919 y 1923, rodeado de empleados públicos, en una fotografía tomada en 1919. Foto cortesía Héctor Lindo.

La década de 1920 en El Salvador fue particularmente notoria por la corrupción y los escándalos financieros. En 1922, debido a una crisis económica mundial, bajos precios del café y las consecuencias de una política monetaria poco atinada, bajaron los ingresos tributarios en concepto de impuestos de aduana. El gobierno se vio corto de fondos, con frecuencia dejaba de pagar a los empleados públicos y se vio obligado a conseguir grandes préstamos en el extranjero. Nada de esto puso freno al deseo de altos personajes de aprovechar el control del Estado para el enriquecimiento personal. Su ingenio para aprovecharse de las arcas de la nación se adaptaba a las circunstancias del momento. La corrupción podía tomar varias formas.

Un caso notorio fue un conflicto de intereses de proporciones históricas. Para contratar el [empréstito de 1922](http://www.afehc-historia-centroamericana.org/?action=fi_aff&id=3934) con bancos estadounidenses, el delegado salvadoreño en las negociaciones crediticias era René Keilhauer. Lo interesante del caso es que Keilhauer trabajaba como empleado de un agente de las casas bancarias, Minor Keith, a su vez dueño de la United Fruit Company.

El empleado, un alsaciano, negociaba el futuro económico de El Salvador con su jefe, un estadounidense. Para dar un poco de contexto, las reuniones privadas entre Minor Keith y el presidente Jorge Meléndez siempre tenían como resultado ventajas para las subsidiarias de la United Fruit Company. No hay evidencia contundente de cómo se beneficiaba el señor presidente, pero uno de los temas de la correspondencia privada entre Keilhauer y Keith era decidir cuándo era conveniente sobornar a los políticos centroamericanos. Keith viajó expresamente desde su sede en Nueva York para discutir con Meléndez la mejor forma en la que podía aprovechar sus conexiones en Wall Street para que El Salvador consiguiera crédito en Estados Unidos. Las condiciones del contrato final fueron en extremo onerosas para el país.

Como indican los siguientes documentos, la corrupción podía tomar otras formas, incluyendo robo en las aduanas y el lucro aprovechando la angustia económica de los empleados públicos.

El primer documento que se presenta a continuación, un informe del representante diplomático Montgomery Schuyler, está vinculado con la aprobación del empréstito de 1922. En esa época, la condición estándar de los banqueros estadounidenses para conceder préstamos a países latinoamericanos era tomar control de la administración de los impuestos aduaneros. Esta medida era parte de la llamada “diplomacia del dólar”, diseñada por el presidente Taft.

En circunstancias en que El Salvador estaba a punto de aceptar este tipo de control, resultaba un poco feo que los administradores de aduanas locales se jactaran de su ingenio en el manejo de los fondos. Esto llevó a la sustitución del administrador de aduanas de Sonsonate, que manejaba de manera escandalosa las jugosas entradas del puerto de Acajutla.

\*\*\*

**Documento 1 \***

San Salvador, El Salvador, a 1 de julio de 1922  
Excelentísimo secretario de Estado  
Washington

Señor:

Tengo el honor de informar los siguientes acontecimientos de importancia para la semana que terminó el viernes 30 de junio de 1922:

\[…\]

Por orden del Ministro de Hacienda, fechada el 30 de junio y publicada en el _Diario Oficial_ del mismo día, se anuncia que el señor Salvador Mendoza ha sido nombrado administrador de la aduana de Sonsonate. El actual administrador, el Sr. Francisco Urrutia, está a punto de “pasar a otro puesto en la administración pública”. La reputación del Sr. Urrutia ha sido notoria durante el año pasado debido a la corrupción y latrocinio extraordinariamente abiertos que han caracterizado su administración en Sonsonate. He advertido varias veces al presidente que la permanencia en el puesto \[de Urrutia\] estaba perjudicando mucho el buen nombre del gobierno salvadoreño. El señor Urrutia, sin embargo, era el protegido personal favorito de Doña Mercedes de Meléndez, la madre del presidente, y del doctor Quiñónez, vicepresidente, de quien había sido valet. El asunto se había convertido en un escándalo tal, que ‘Chico’ Urrutia, como se le llama, ha estado bromeando en público al respecto y recientemente dijo que, desde la designación de un nuevo administrador en La Unión, él era ahora, con mucho, el más honesto de los administradores de aduanas del país. Se cree que su renuncia en este momento se debe a su temor de que bajo la inspección de aduanas que se establecerá si se aprueba el nuevo préstamo, se examinará su contabilidad con algún cuidado.

Tengo el honor de ser, señor, su atento y seguro servidor.

Montgomery Schuyler

\*\*\*

El segundo documento es un informe diplomático que describe la práctica de los “vales”. Debido a la crisis económica, el gobierno no tenía dinero efectivo, de forma que entregaba pagarés a los empleados públicos. Los empleados, que vivían siempre cortos de fondos, estaban apurados por obtener dinero para alimentar a sus familias y aceptaban descuentos con tal de ver los colones contantes y sonantes. Individuos vinculados al régimen aprovechaban la desesperación de los empleados para quedarse con la mitad de su salario.

**Documento 2 \***

San Salvador,

27 de octubre de 1922  
Excelentísimo secretario de Estado  
Washington

Señor:

Tengo la honra de informar de la siguiente manera sobre la semana que terminó el jueves 26 de octubre:

\[…\]

Como se indicó en mi expediente número 218 del 6 de octubre, debido a las dificultades financieras del gobierno, a la mayoría de sus empleados se les paga mediante pagarés, que se descuentan a un tipo de interés exorbitante, frecuentemente hasta el 50%. Estos pagarés se llaman “vales”. Parece que a menudo se venden a comisionistas que esperan en las aceras fuera de las oficinas del gobierno, quienes a su vez los traspasan a personas que tienen influencia con el gobierno. Parece que estos últimos individuos aseguran su pago de las arcas del Estado, más o menos prontamente, al valor nominal. Se dice que un exalcalde de San Salvador y algunos de los altos funcionarios del gobierno están involucrados en este tráfico sórdido, que está asumiendo rápidamente las proporciones de un escándalo público.

\[…\]

Tengo el honor de ser, señor, su atento y seguro servidor.

Clarence B. Hewes

\*\*\*

\* La fuente para ambos documentos es: National Archives Microfilm Publications. Records of the Department of State Relating to Internal Affairs of El Salvador, 1910– 29, Roll 3, Political Affairs.
