**Pío Romero Bosque** ([Suchitoto](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suchitoto "Suchitoto"), [El Salvador](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Salvador "El Salvador"), 13 de febrero de 1861-[Managua](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Managua "Managua"), 10 de diciembre de 1935) fue un [político](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pol%C3%ADtico "Político") y [abogado](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abogado "Abogado") salvadoreño, quien fue [Presidente de El Salvador](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presidente_de_El_Salvador "Presidente de El Salvador") desde 1927 hasta 1931.

En 1892 inició una larga carrera política al ser elegido diputado a la Asamblea Nacional. También sirvió como juez de primera instancia y magistrado en el poder judicial. En el 23 de marzo de 1901, la Asamblea Nacional Legislativa eligió los Magistrados de la [Corte Suprema de Justicia](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corte_Suprema_de_Justicia_de_El_Salvador "Corte Suprema de Justicia de El Salvador") y Cámaras Seccionales, siendo Tercer Magistrado en la Cámara Primera de Segunda Instancia el Dr. Pío Romero Bosque.[\[1\]](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/P%C3%ADo_Romero_Bosque#cite_note-1)​ En el gobierno de los presidentes [Jorge Meléndez](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jorge_Mel%C3%A9ndez_Ram%C3%ADrez "Jorge Meléndez Ramírez") (1919-1923) y [Alfonso Quiñónez Molina](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfonso_Qui%C3%B1%C3%B3nez_Molina "Alfonso Quiñónez Molina") (1923-1927) ocupó los cargos de Ministro de Guerra y Ministro de Gobernación.

[![Image 3](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b6/Miembros_del_Gabinete_y_Ejercito_del_Gobierno_del_Dr._Alfonso_Qui%C3%B1onez_Molina_%E2%80%93_1926.jpg/250px-Miembros_del_Gabinete_y_Ejercito_del_Gobierno_del_Dr._Alfonso_Qui%C3%B1onez_Molina_%E2%80%93_1926.jpg)](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archivo:Miembros_del_Gabinete_y_Ejercito_del_Gobierno_del_Dr._Alfonso_Qui%C3%B1onez_Molina_%E2%80%93_1926.jpg)

Miembros del Gabinete y Ejército del Gobierno del Dr. Alfonso Quiñonez Molina, a la derecha su sucesor Pio Romero Bosque.

Después de la ruina ocasionada por el terremoto del 28 de abril de 1919 en San Salvador, formó parte del Comité Central encargado de la construcción de barracas como su secretario.[\[2\]](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/P%C3%ADo_Romero_Bosque#cite_note-2)​

[![Image 4](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/42/Supreme_Court_of_Justice_of_El_Salvador_%28c._1914%E2%80%931916%29.png/250px-Supreme_Court_of_Justice_of_El_Salvador_%28c._1914%E2%80%931916%29.png)](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archivo:Supreme_Court_of_Justice_of_El_Salvador_/(c._1914%E2%80%931916/).png)

Pio Romero Bosque. Fue uno de los Magistrados de la [Corte Suprema de Justicia](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corte_Suprema_de_Justicia_de_El_Salvador "Corte Suprema de Justicia de El Salvador") y Cámaras Seccionales, siendo Tercer Magistrado en la Cámara Primera de Segunda Instancia el Dr. Pío Romero Bosque.

la dinastía Quiñónez instaló al hermano menor de Carlos, Jorge, como candidato presidencial del Partido Nacional Demócrata, pero su candidatura fue impugnada por el terrateniente Arturo Araujo del Partido Laborista Salvadoreño (PLS). Jorge y Quiñónez hizo que el presidente de la Corte Suprema, Pío Romero Bosque, anunciara su propia candidatura y procedieron a manipular las elecciones para que Jorge llegara en primer lugar, Romero en segundo y Araujo en tercero. Jorge y Quiñónez asumieron el cargo en marzo de 1919 como presidente y vicepresidente, respectivamente, y gobernarían El Salvador hasta 1927.

"Se planificó cuidadosamente que el Dr. Pío Romero Bosque recibiera el segundo mayor número de votos y, en consecuencia, los votantes fueron enviados por el Meléndez-Quinonez Partido para emitir sus votos por el Dr. Bosque."

—16 de enero de 1919 Frank D. Arnold embajador de Los Estados Unidos en El Salvador [\[3\]](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/P%C3%ADo_Romero_Bosque#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChing1997250%E2%80%93251-3)​

### Presidencia de Pío Romero Bosque

\[[editar](https://es.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=P%C3%ADo_Romero_Bosque&action=edit&section=2 "Editar sección: Presidencia de Pío Romero Bosque")\]

[![Image 5](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/6c/P%C3%ADo_Romero_Bosque_as_Vice_President_of_El_Salvador.png/250px-P%C3%ADo_Romero_Bosque_as_Vice_President_of_El_Salvador.png)](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archivo:P%C3%ADo_Romero_Bosque_as_Vice_President_of_El_Salvador.png)

Pío Romero Bosque (1 de marzo de 1927 – 1 de marzo de 1931. Partido PND). Marcó el final de la dinastía Meléndez-Quiñones. Fue un vástago de la "dinastía Meléndez-Quiñónez", que en lugar de imponer su propio heredero como Presidente, permitió una democratización del país con sus primeras elecciones libres en 1931, ganadas por Arturo Araújo.

Pese a no pertenecer a la familia Meléndez-Quiñones, se le considera parte de la dinastía puesto que era el médico particular familiar. Ascendió al poder mediante el apoyo de la familia gobernante el 1 de marzo de 1927 tras haberse desempeñado como ministro de guerra.[\[4\]](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/P%C3%ADo_Romero_Bosque#cite_note-cuscatla-4)​ Con el apoyo de la familia Meléndez-Quiñónez fue elegido presidente de la República. Tomó posesión del cargo el 1 de marzo de 1927, en medio de un clima de represión política. Sin embargo, ya en el poder, tomó medidas contrarias a los intereses de la familia Meléndez, lo cual orilló a la oligarquía a un fallido [golpe de Estado](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golpe_de_Estado "Golpe de Estado") en 1931. Sin embargo ya en la presidencia se generó un descontento entre la familia Meléndez-Quiñonez, el expresidente [Jorge Meléndez](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jorge_Mel%C3%A9ndez_Ram%C3%ADrez "Jorge Meléndez Ramírez") y [Alfonso Quiñonez](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfonso_Qui%C3%B1%C3%B3nez_Molina "Alfonso Quiñónez Molina"), intentaron realizar un [golpe de Estado](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golpes_de_Estado_en_El_Salvador "Golpes de Estado en El Salvador") hacia Pío Romero Bosque, lo cual resultó en un fracaso y Quiñonez junto a Meléndez terminaron exiliándose hacia [Costa Rica](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Costa_Rica "Costa Rica"). Bosque prosiguió con su gobierno hasta 1931, lo cual abrió las puertas hacia un periodo democrático, durante su gobierno se dio autonomía a la [Universidad de El Salvador](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universidad_de_El_Salvador "Universidad de El Salvador"), se creó la [Asociación General de Estudiantes Universitarios Salvadoreños](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asociaci%C3%B3n_General_de_Estudiantes_Universitarios_Salvadore%C3%B1os "Asociación General de Estudiantes Universitarios Salvadoreños"), (AGEUS), permitió la legalización de varios partidos políticos entre ellos el [Partido Comunista Salvadoreño](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Partido_Comunista_Salvadore%C3%B1o "Partido Comunista Salvadoreño") entre otros logros, sin embargo durante su gobierno también lidió con varias manifestaciones producidas en algunas ciudades de El Salvador, por diversos motivos las cuales fueron reprimidas, Al inicio de la presidencia de Romero, los precios del café eran altos y las exportaciones de café de El Salvador alcanzaban cifras récord. Mientras tanto, Romero heredó un déficit presupuestario y una deuda de SV₡23.8 millones de su predecesor que resultó de la emisión de una gran cantidad de bonos fiscales. En el discurso inaugural de Romero, declaró que tenía la intención de solucionar la situación financiera del país. En 1927, implementó varios impuestos nuevos sobre las importaciones para aumentar la financiación del gobierno y el ejército. También implementó un impuesto sobre todas las tiendas generales operadas por hombres en un esfuerzo por promover la participación de las mujeres en la economía. Romero concedió exenciones fiscales en el cultivo de ciertos cultivos debido al descontento de los trabajadores agrícolas respecto a las tasas impositivas. El comercio internacional con Guatemala y Honduras también recibió exenciones fiscales. El Ministerio de Finanzas informó que las reformas implementadas en 1927 y 1928 tuvieron impactos positivos en la economía del país, ya que la producción económica aumentó. [\[5\]](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/P%C3%ADo_Romero_Bosque#cite_note-lasbiograf%C3%ADas.com-5)​ Tomó medidas tales como la redistribución de la tierra, la cual fue una de las causas del [levantamiento campesino](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Levantamiento_campesino_en_El_Salvador_de_1932 "Levantamiento campesino en El Salvador de 1932") de años más tarde; así como la libertad de prensa; la libertad de asociación; la no persecución a la oposición; y, además, convoca a elecciones libres, las cuales no fueron manipuladas y fueron respetadas.[\[6\]](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/P%C3%ADo_Romero_Bosque#cite_note-UES-6)​[\[7\]](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/P%C3%ADo_Romero_Bosque#cite_note-Thomas-7)​ Tras acabar su periodo entregó la presidencia a [Arturo Araujo](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arturo_Araujo "Arturo Araujo"), triunfante en las elecciones, el 1 de marzo de 1931, acabando así la dinastía. Durante el final de su presidencia se produjo la [Gran depresión](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gran_depresi%C3%B3n "Gran depresión") de 1929. Dado que El Salvador dependía mucho de la economía estadounidense, el país se vio muy gravemente afectado, sufriendo principalmente por la dramática caída de los precios del café exacerbando la crisis en la sociedad salvadoreña. Durante el gobierno del Dr. Romero Bosque (1927-1931) el movimiento sindical llega a abarcar a los trabajadores de la ciudad y a los obreros agrícolas. Se crean sindicatos en las ciudades, pueblos, fincas, etc. Además, a los campesinos pobres y acomodados se les organiza en ligas campesinas y cooperativas. Esto constituyó una conquista muy importante. El movimiento campesino adquirió proporciones no igualadas hasta el momento. La consigna central de “La Regional” fue la lucha por la reforma agraria democrática, considerando como tal el reparto de tierras a los campesinos, la destrucción de los latifundios y la erradicación de las formas feudales de explotación; el desarrollo del crédito agrícola, la proporción de ayuda técnica y de abonos, de semillas e instrumentos de labor. Tales eran las reivindicaciones más sentidas y que su realización se anhelaba a fin de elevar el nivel de vida de los campesinos y abrir el camino de la industrialización nacional. Asimismo, se luchaba por objetivos más inmediatos, como eran la rebaja de los alquileres de la tierra, el aumento de los salarios en las labores agrícolas, el cese de los despidos injustificados, la abolición de los maltratos de obra a los trabajadores y de las injusticias cometidas por los hacendados y sus empleados.

[![Image 6](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f9/P%C3%ADo_Romero_Bosque_and_his_family.png/250px-P%C3%ADo_Romero_Bosque_and_his_family.png)](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archivo:P%C3%ADo_Romero_Bosque_and_his_family.png)

Pío Romero Bosque y su familia

En los primeros tiempos, el gobierno del Dr. Romero Bosque respetó los derechos democráticos. Los obreros se organizaron sin dificultades. Se refiere que el presidente en repetidas ocasiones, ofreció su contribución monetaria para el sostenimiento de la FRTS, pero ésta siempre declinó la aceptación. Por esta época resultaba extraño para nadie que el Dr. Romero convocara a su despacho presidencial a los dirigentes obreros para platicar con ellos. No fueron pocas las oportunidades en que les expresó que estaba de acuerdo con la organización de los obreros pero no con la movilización y organización de los trabajadores del campo. “Los obreros hacen mal con inquietar a los campesinos, ya que estos viven tranquilos en la situación en que se encuentran”, les decía. Es dentro de este formidable ascenso de la lucha de masas, que en el mes de marzo de 1930 se funda el Partido Comunista de El Salvador. Por estas fechas Agustín Farabundo Martí estaba ausente del país.

[![Image 7](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/76/El_salvador_presidente_araujo_toma_la_presidencia_1930.jpg/330px-El_salvador_presidente_araujo_toma_la_presidencia_1930.jpg)](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archivo:El_salvador_presidente_araujo_toma_la_presidencia_1930.jpg)

Toma de posesión de Arturo Araujo como presidente de El Salvador, Destaca el presidente saliente Pío Romero Bosque y Entonces Vicepresidente Brigadier Martínez el 1 de marzo de 1931

Frente a la deteriorada situación económica surgieron las primeras agrupaciones de trabajadores y se sucedieron las huelgas. En 1930 se fundó el [Partido Comunista Salvadoreño](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Partido_Comunista_Salvadore%C3%B1o "Partido Comunista Salvadoreño"). Romero Bosque reprimió duramente las protestas pero al final de su mandato, organizó unas elecciones consideradas libres y entregó el poder al candidato ganador, [Arturo Araujo](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arturo_Araujo "Arturo Araujo") el 1 de marzo de 1931.

Sus políticas sobre la posesión de la tierra fueron un elemento que provocó el [levantamiento campesino de 1932](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Levantamiento_campesino_de_1932_/(El_Salvador/) "Levantamiento campesino de 1932 (El Salvador)") El autor británico Alastair White describió la presidencia de Romero como "el comienzo de un período de transición que terminó con la supresión de la rebelión de 1932, después de la cual el nuevo orden de cosas fue evidente". El autor estadounidense Thomas P. Anderson escribió que Romero es recordado en El Salvador como "una especie de Buen Rey Wenceslao salvadoreño" y describió su presidencia como una "edad dorada en la problemática historia del país". Por otro lado, el editorialista conservador salvadoreño Juan Ulloa culpó a las reformas democráticas de Romero como la causa directa de La Matanza, una rebelión de 1932 dirigida por Martí y el PCES, seguida de los asesinatos masivos de hasta 40,000 personas. Ulloa también acusó a Romero de "conocer a sus líderes \[comunistas\]"..

"Hago este llamado formal a nuestro patriotismo para que en este próximo paso para resolver el problema político de la sucesión presidencial, estemos listos para apoyar, de cualquier manera posible, la forma que toma este proceso, como un reflejo de nuestra prudencia y confirmación de nuestra preparación para una vida democrática."

—22 de abril de 1930[\[8\]](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/P%C3%ADo_Romero_Bosque#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChing1997344-8)​

Tiene fama de ser uno de los pocos, si no el único, presidente salvadoreño que fue capaz de alcanzar un equilibrio político en el gobierno durante su administración. Este equilibrio se conoce a menudo como el "Mix natural", un equilibrio entre la concesión a las demandas de los diversos componentes de la sociedad y la represión de la misma en un país determinado. Fue un vástago de la [dinastía Meléndez-Quiñones](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dinast%C3%ADa_Mel%C3%A9ndez-Qui%C3%B1ones "Dinastía Meléndez-Quiñones"), que en lugar de imponer su propio heredero como Presidente, permitió una democratización del país con sus primeras [elecciones libres en 1931](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elecci%C3%B3n_presidencial_de_El_Salvador_de_1931 "Elección presidencial de El Salvador de 1931"). Esta sería la primera [elección democrática](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elecciones "Elecciones") en [El Salvador](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Salvador "El Salvador") desde la [Independencia de la Corona Española en 1821](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Independencia_de_Centroam%C3%A9rica "Independencia de Centroamérica") dando así también el fin de la [República Cafetalera](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Historia_de_El_Salvador "Historia de El Salvador") en [El Salvador](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Salvador "El Salvador") en el que los [Terratenientes](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Terrateniente "Terrateniente") ya no ocuparían los cargos en la [presidencia de la república](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presidente_de_El_Salvador "Presidente de El Salvador") dando así el inicio del [Militarismo](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Militarismo "Militarismo").

[![Image 8](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/ef/Tumba_De_Pio_Romero_Bosque._En_El_Cementerio_Los_Ilustes.jpg/250px-Tumba_De_Pio_Romero_Bosque._En_El_Cementerio_Los_Ilustes.jpg)](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archivo:Tumba_De_Pio_Romero_Bosque._En_El_Cementerio_Los_Ilustes.jpg)

Tumba de Pío Romero Bosque en el Cementerio de Los Ilustres.

La United Fruit Company y el empréstito de 1922 en El Salvador por Héctor Lindo-Fuentes
=======================================================================================

**Publicado:** 15.05.2015 | **Autor:** [sriaamhe](https://blogdelaamhe.wordpress.com/author/sriaamhe/ "Entradas de sriaamhe") | **Archivado en:** [Papers](https://blogdelaamhe.wordpress.com/category/papers/) |Comentarios desactivados en La United Fruit Company y el empréstito de 1922 en El Salvador por Héctor Lindo-FuentesLa historia política del empréstito de 1922 coloca a la presidencia de Jorge Meléndez en la categoría de una de las más dañinas en la historia de El Salvador. Un estudio de las negociaciones muestra que, contrario a lo que dice la narrativa tradicional, la United Fruit Company, y su dueño Minor Keith, tuvieron un influencia grande en El Salvador en la década de los veinte. Como resultado del empréstito El Salvador comprometió el 70% de sus impuestos de aduana al pago de la deuda a banqueros estadounidenses y aceptó la presencia de un «representante fiscal» que supervisó el cobro de impuestos y tuvo gran injerencia en la política económica del país.  
[http://www.afehc-historia-centroamericana.org/index.php?action=fi\_aff&id=3934](http://www.afehc-historia-centroamericana.org/index.php?action=fi_aff&id=3934)

**Pío Romero Bosque** (1860 – 10 December 1935), contemporarily referred to as **Don Pío**,[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P%C3%ADo_Romero_Bosque#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHaggerty199014-2)[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P%C3%ADo_Romero_Bosque#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAnderson19718-3)[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P%C3%ADo_Romero_Bosque#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhite197397-4) was a Salvadoran politician and lawyer who served as [President of El Salvador](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_El_Salvador "President of El Salvador") from 1927 to 1931. He had previously served as [Alfonso Quiñónez Molina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfonso_Qui%C3%B1%C3%B3nez_Molina "Alfonso Quiñónez Molina")'s [Vice President](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_President_of_El_Salvador "Vice President of El Salvador") from 1923 to 1927 and as El Salvador's [Minister of War, the Navy, and Aviation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minister_of_National_Defense_/(El_Salvador/) "Minister of National Defense (El Salvador)") (Minister of War) from 1919 to 1927.

Romero completed his [Doctor of Law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doctor_of_Law "Doctor of Law") in 1889 and was shortly afterwards appointed by the [Supreme Court of Justice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supreme_Court_of_Justice_of_El_Salvador "Supreme Court of Justice of El Salvador") to serve as a judge. He served as a judge in [San Salvador](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Salvador "San Salvador") and [Zacatecoluca](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zacatecoluca "Zacatecoluca") during the 1890s and 1900s and also served as a magistrate on the Supreme Court of Justice itself from 1893 to 1895 and again from 1899 to 1903. He also briefly served as a deputy of the [Legislative Assembly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Legislative_Assembly_of_El_Salvador "Legislative Assembly of El Salvador") from 1892 to 1893 before resigning to serve on the Supreme Court of Justice. From 1903 to 1907, Romero served as the [Minister of Governance, Development, and Public Instruction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ministry_of_the_Interior_/(El_Salvador/) "Ministry of the Interior (El Salvador)") under President [Pedro José Escalón](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pedro_Jos%C3%A9_Escal%C3%B3n "Pedro José Escalón"). From 1914 to 1919, he served as the president of the Supreme Court of Justice.

Romero became President of El Salvador in 1927. El Salvador's economy early in Romero's government benefited from high coffee prices and taxation reforms, but the [Great Depression](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Depression "Great Depression") and the collapse of coffee prices crippled El Salvador's economy as it was heavily dependent on coffee exports. Romero distanced himself from the [Meléndez–Quiñónez dynasty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mel%C3%A9ndez%E2%80%93Qui%C3%B1%C3%B3nez_dynasty "Meléndez–Quiñónez dynasty") that preceded him and implemented various democratic reforms. Romero's government survived an attempted coup by supporters of the Meléndez–Quiñónez [political dynasty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Political_dynasty "Political dynasty") in December 1927. Romero did not hand-pick a presidential successor as his predecessors had done and was succeeded by [Arturo Araujo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arturo_Araujo "Arturo Araujo") who won the [1931 presidential election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1931_Salvadoran_presidential_election "1931 Salvadoran presidential election"), considered by historians to be El Salvador's first free and fair democratic election. Romero fled El Salvador during the presidency of General [Maximiliano Hernández Martínez](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maximiliano_Hern%C3%A1ndez_Mart%C3%ADnez "Maximiliano Hernández Martínez"), whose government reversed all of Romero's democratic reforms after [overthrowing Araujo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1931_Salvadoran_coup_d%27%C3%A9tat "1931 Salvadoran coup d'état") in late 1931. Romero died in exile in Nicaragua in 1935.

Pío Romero Bosque was born in 1860 in [Suchitoto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suchitoto "Suchitoto"), El Salvador, to Serapío Romero and Rosario Bosque.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P%C3%ADo_Romero_Bosque#cite_note-FOOTNOTELeistenschneiderLeistenschneider1980183-5)[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P%C3%ADo_Romero_Bosque#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMart%C3%ADnez_Pe%C3%B1ateS%C3%A1nchez2004461-6)[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P%C3%ADo_Romero_Bosque#cite_note-FOOTNOTECortez_Tejada2023139-7) Bosque was of [Spanish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spaniards "Spaniards") descent.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P%C3%ADo_Romero_Bosque#cite_note-FOOTNOTELa_Prensa_Gr%C3%A1fica2005-8) Through Romero's mother, he was a descendant of [Cayetano Bosque](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Cayetano_Bosque&action=edit&redlink=1 "Cayetano Bosque (page does not exist)"), a liberal who served as [Minister of War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minister_of_National_Defense_/(El_Salvador/) "Minister of National Defense (El Salvador)") in 1858. Romero was a landowner, owning a [hacienda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hacienda "Hacienda") in [San Salvador](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Salvador "San Salvador") and [Santiago Nonualco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santiago_Nonualco "Santiago Nonualco") named "El Rosario" and "Nahualapa", respectively.[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P%C3%ADo_Romero_Bosque#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChing1997288%E2%80%93289-9)

Romero completed his bachelor's degree at the Ciencias y Letras college of [Santa Tecla](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santa_Tecla,_El_Salvador "Santa Tecla, El Salvador") and completed his [Doctor of Law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doctor_of_Law "Doctor of Law") at the [University of El Salvador](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_El_Salvador "University of El Salvador") in 1889.[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P%C3%ADo_Romero_Bosque#cite_note-FOOTNOTECortez_Tejada2023139-7)[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P%C3%ADo_Romero_Bosque#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWard1916172-10) Later that year, the [Supreme Court of Justice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supreme_Court_of_Justice_of_El_Salvador "Supreme Court of Justice of El Salvador") appointed Romero to serve as the supplementary judge of the 1st circuit of the [San Salvador Department](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Salvador_Department "San Salvador Department"). A few months after this appointment, he was named as the proprietary judge of the [Zacatecoluca](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zacatecoluca "Zacatecoluca") district; he served in this position for two years.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P%C3%ADo_Romero_Bosque#cite_note-FOOTNOTELeistenschneiderLeistenschneider1980183-5)

In 1892 and 1893, Romero was elected as a deputy of the [Legislative Assembly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Legislative_Assembly_of_El_Salvador "Legislative Assembly of El Salvador"). He resigned in 1893 following his appointment as the fourth magistrate of the Supreme Court of Justice. His term ended in 1895 and he resumed his role as the proprietary judge of Zacatecoluca until 1899.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P%C3%ADo_Romero_Bosque#cite_note-FOOTNOTELeistenschneiderLeistenschneider1980183-5) Romero served a second term as a supreme court magistrate from 1899 until 14 April 1903.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P%C3%ADo_Romero_Bosque#cite_note-FOOTNOTELeistenschneiderLeistenschneider1980184-11) In 1914, Romero became the [president of the Supreme Court of Justice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_the_Supreme_Court_of_Justice_of_El_Salvador "President of the Supreme Court of Justice of El Salvador") ([es](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anexo:Presidentes_de_la_Corte_Suprema_de_Justicia_de_El_Salvador "es:Anexo:Presidentes de la Corte Suprema de Justicia de El Salvador")); he served in this position until 1919.[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P%C3%ADo_Romero_Bosque#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChing1997288-12)

[![Image 3: A portrait photograph of Pío Romero Bosque](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/6c/P%C3%ADo_Romero_Bosque_as_Vice_President_of_El_Salvador.png/250px-P%C3%ADo_Romero_Bosque_as_Vice_President_of_El_Salvador.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:P%C3%ADo_Romero_Bosque_as_Vice_President_of_El_Salvador.png)

Romero as [Vice President of El Salvador](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_President_of_El_Salvador "Vice President of El Salvador") (c. 1923–1925)[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P%C3%ADo_Romero_Bosque#cite_note-FOOTNOTEConsulate_General_of_El_Salvador192511-13)

On 12 March 1903, President [Pedro José Escalón](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pedro_Jos%C3%A9_Escal%C3%B3n "Pedro José Escalón") appointed Romero as El Salvador's Vice Secretary of Governance and Development, and later that year he was promoted to serve as [Minister of Governance, Development, and Public Instruction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ministry_of_the_Interior_/(El_Salvador/) "Ministry of the Interior (El Salvador)"), succeeding Doctor [José Rosa Pacas](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Jos%C3%A9_Rosa_Pacas&action=edit&redlink=1 "José Rosa Pacas (page does not exist)").[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P%C3%ADo_Romero_Bosque#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChing1997288-12)[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P%C3%ADo_Romero_Bosque#cite_note-FOOTNOTELeistenschneiderLeistenschneider1980161_&_184-14) During the [1919 presidential election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1919_Salvadoran_presidential_election "1919 Salvadoran presidential election"), President [Alfonso Quiñónez Molina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfonso_Qui%C3%B1%C3%B3nez_Molina "Alfonso Quiñónez Molina") (who was Romero's brother-in-law)[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P%C3%ADo_Romero_Bosque#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurns1984307-15) and presidential front-runner [Jorge Meléndez](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jorge_Mel%C3%A9ndez "Jorge Meléndez") installed Romero as a presidential candidate in order to receive more votes than [Arturo Araujo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arturo_Araujo "Arturo Araujo"), another presidential candidate, in an effort to humiliate Araujo for attempting to challenge Jorge's presidential bid.[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P%C3%ADo_Romero_Bosque#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChing1997250-16) Quiñónez's government sent telegrams to polling stations across El Salvador instructing them to rig votes in favor of Meléndez first and Romero second.[\[17\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P%C3%ADo_Romero_Bosque#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChing1997250%E2%80%93251-17) Romero came in second place, receiving 4,370 votes to Jorge's 166,441 votes and Araujo's 1,022 votes. Upon assuming the presidency, Jorge appointed Romero as the minister of war, the navy, and aviation (minister of war).[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P%C3%ADo_Romero_Bosque#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChing1997251-18)

During the [1923 presidential election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1923_Salvadoran_presidential_election "1923 Salvadoran presidential election"), Romero was elected to serve as Quiñónez's [Vice President](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_President_of_El_Salvador "Vice President of El Salvador"). Upon assuming office on 1 March 1923, Quiñonez appointed Romero to continue serving as Minister of War,[\[19\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P%C3%ADo_Romero_Bosque#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChing1997280-19) an office he would hold until 1927.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P%C3%ADo_Romero_Bosque#cite_note-FOOTNOTELeistenschneiderLeistenschneider1980184-11) As Minister of War, Romero implemented military reforms that improved training standards.[\[20\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P%C3%ADo_Romero_Bosque#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAnderson197141-20) On 26 January 1927, Romero issued a decree that renamed the country's military academy to the [Captain General Gerardo Barrios Military School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Captain_General_Gerardo_Barrios_Military_School "Captain General Gerardo Barrios Military School").[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P%C3%ADo_Romero_Bosque#cite_note-FOOTNOTELeistenschneiderLeistenschneider1980184-11) Romero forged a strong relationship with the Salvadoran military while holding his minister position.[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P%C3%ADo_Romero_Bosque#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChing1997334-21)

In 1926, as [the following year's presidential election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1927_Salvadoran_presidential_election "1927 Salvadoran presidential election") approached, Quiñónez hand-picked Romero to succeed him as president. Romero ran for office unopposed and won the election unanimously on 13 January 1927 as a member of the ruling [National Democratic Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Democratic_Party_/(El_Salvador/) "National Democratic Party (El Salvador)") (PND).[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P%C3%ADo_Romero_Bosque#cite_note-FOOTNOTECortez_Tejada2023139-7)[\[22\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P%C3%ADo_Romero_Bosque#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChing1997286-22)[\[23\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P%C3%ADo_Romero_Bosque#cite_note-FOOTNOTERoyal_Institute_of_International_Affairs192716-23) [Gustavo Vides](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gustavo_Vides "Gustavo Vides"), an engineer, was elected as Romero's vice president; Quiñónez also hand-picked Vides, who previously served as Quiñónez's [Minister of Finance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ministry_of_Finance_/(El_Salvador/) "Ministry of Finance (El Salvador)").[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P%C3%ADo_Romero_Bosque#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChing1997305%E2%80%93306-24)

[![Image 4: A black-and-white photograph of Pío Romero Bosque facing the camera and wearing the Salvadoran presidential sash](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f0/Official_portrait_of_President_P%C3%ADo_Romero_Bosque.png/250px-Official_portrait_of_President_P%C3%ADo_Romero_Bosque.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Official_portrait_of_President_P%C3%ADo_Romero_Bosque.png)

Official portrait of Romero taken on 1 March 1927 by the _El Día_ newspaper[\[25\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P%C3%ADo_Romero_Bosque#cite_note-FOOTNOTECortez_Tejada2023142-25)

Romero assumed the presidency on 1 March 1927 between 9 and 10 a.m. [CST](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Time_Zone "Central Time Zone").[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P%C3%ADo_Romero_Bosque#cite_note-FOOTNOTECortez_Tejada2023140-26) He appointed the following individuals to his cabinet: Doctor [José Gustavo Guerrero](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jos%C3%A9_Gustavo_Guerrero "José Gustavo Guerrero") as [Minister of Foreign Relations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_ministers_of_foreign_affairs_of_El_Salvador "List of ministers of foreign affairs of El Salvador");[\[a\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P%C3%ADo_Romero_Bosque#cite_note-27) Doctor [Manuel Vicente Mendoza](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Manuel_Vicente_Mendoza&action=edit&redlink=1 "Manuel Vicente Mendoza (page does not exist)") as Minister of Governance, Development, Agriculture, and Labor; and Doctor [Alberto Gómez Zárate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alberto_G%C3%B3mez_Z%C3%A1rate "Alberto Gómez Zárate") as Minister of War, the Navy, and Aviation.[\[b\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P%C3%ADo_Romero_Bosque#cite_note-28)[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P%C3%ADo_Romero_Bosque#cite_note-FOOTNOTELeistenschneiderLeistenschneider1980184-11) Romero was an [economic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fiscal_conservatism "Fiscal conservatism") and [social conservative](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_conservative "Social conservative"),[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P%C3%ADo_Romero_Bosque#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAnderson19718-3) unlike all his predecessors dating back to 1871 who were all idealist or pragmatic [liberals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liberalism "Liberalism").[\[27\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P%C3%ADo_Romero_Bosque#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhite197387%E2%80%9388-29)

### Anticipation of a puppet presidency

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=P%C3%ADo_Romero_Bosque&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Anticipation of a puppet presidency")\]

Quiñónez hand-picked Romero as his successor believing him to be a trusted collaborator who would continue the [Meléndez–Quiñónez dynasty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mel%C3%A9ndez%E2%80%93Qui%C3%B1%C3%B3nez_dynasty "Meléndez–Quiñónez dynasty"),[\[28\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P%C3%ADo_Romero_Bosque#cite_note-FOOTNOTELindo_FuentesChingLara_Mart%C3%ADnez200779-30) a [political dynasty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Political_dynasty "Political dynasty") that had ruled El Salvador since [Carlos Meléndez](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carlos_Mel%C3%A9ndez_/(politician/) "Carlos Meléndez (politician)") became president in 1913.[\[29\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P%C3%ADo_Romero_Bosque#cite_note-FOOTNOTECortez_Tejada2023139_&_140-31) Romero was chosen to continue the dynasty as neither the Meléndez's nor the Quiñónez's had any family members who were eligible or willing to become the next president of El Salvador.[\[28\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P%C3%ADo_Romero_Bosque#cite_note-FOOTNOTELindo_FuentesChingLara_Mart%C3%ADnez200779-30) Furthermore, Quiñónez intended to be able to control Romero as a [puppet ruler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Puppet_ruler "Puppet ruler").[\[30\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P%C3%ADo_Romero_Bosque#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhite197395-32) Likewise, contemporary public opinion believed that Romero would continue the Meléndez–Quiñónez dynasty's politics and policies during his presidency.[\[31\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P%C3%ADo_Romero_Bosque#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBernal_Ram%C3%ADrezQuijano_de_Batres200994-33)

[Cornelius Van Hemert Engert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cornelius_Van_Hemert_Engert "Cornelius Van Hemert Engert"), the United States _[chargé d'affaires](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charg%C3%A9_d%27affaires "Chargé d'affaires")_ to El Salvador, described Romero as "weak and irresolute". [Jefferson Caffery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jefferson_Caffery "Jefferson Caffery"), the [United States ambassador to El Salvador](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_ambassadors_of_the_United_States_to_El_Salvador "List of ambassadors of the United States to El Salvador"), referred to Romero as a man "of no particular force, and with probably no superfluous amount of backbone". Engert believed that Quiñónez selected Romero to act as a puppet ruler due to his perceived weakness and that Quiñónez would continue to govern the country from [behind the scenes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Power_behind_the_throne "Power behind the throne")[\[32\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P%C3%ADo_Romero_Bosque#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChing1997290-34)[\[33\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P%C3%ADo_Romero_Bosque#cite_note-FOOTNOTEvan_den_Berk2016231-35) as he had been appointed as the [first presidential designate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_El_Salvador#Succession "President of El Salvador"), making Quiñónez second in line to the presidency after Vides.[\[34\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P%C3%ADo_Romero_Bosque#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChing1997305-36)

### Ending the Meléndez–Quiñónez dynasty

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=P%C3%ADo_Romero_Bosque&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Ending the Meléndez–Quiñónez dynasty")\]

[![Image 5: A black-and-white photograph of several men standing and facing the camera](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b6/Miembros_del_Gabinete_y_Ejercito_del_Gobierno_del_Dr._Alfonso_Qui%C3%B1onez_Molina_%E2%80%93_1926.jpg/250px-Miembros_del_Gabinete_y_Ejercito_del_Gobierno_del_Dr._Alfonso_Qui%C3%B1onez_Molina_%E2%80%93_1926.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Miembros_del_Gabinete_y_Ejercito_del_Gobierno_del_Dr._Alfonso_Qui%C3%B1onez_Molina_%E2%80%93_1926.jpg)

Then-Vice President Romero (sixth from the left) with President [Alfonso Quiñónez Molina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfonso_Qui%C3%B1%C3%B3nez_Molina "Alfonso Quiñónez Molina") and other cabinet members in 1926

One month into Romero's presidency, he forced Marcos Letona and Salvador Rivas, the two Vice Secretaries of Development and Public Instruction, to resign despite an agreement between Romero and Quiñónez to maintain certain political appointments in place; Quiñónez, subsequently, accused Romero of failing to uphold his political promises. Engert believed that these decisions were part of Romero's "campaign to do away with the Quinonez \[_[sic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sic "Sic")_\] influence".[\[34\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P%C3%ADo_Romero_Bosque#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChing1997305-36) Romero also lifted a [state of emergency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/State_of_emergency "State of emergency") which was in effect throughout Quiñónez's presidency, ended press [censorship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Censorship "Censorship"), and allowed public demonstrations.[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P%C3%ADo_Romero_Bosque#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChing1997305%E2%80%93306-24) These reforms led to public protests against Quiñónez's appointment as the first presidential designate, and students from the University of El Salvador called for his resignation. After pressure from Romero's supporters, protestors, and even some high-ranking military officers, Quiñónez resigned and left the country for exile in France.[\[35\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P%C3%ADo_Romero_Bosque#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChing1997306-37)

In December 1927, Jorge, Quiñónez, and their allies plotted a [coup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coup_d%27%C3%A9tat "Coup d'état") to overthrow Romero in an attempt to continue the political dynasty that their families had created.[\[36\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P%C3%ADo_Romero_Bosque#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChing1997308%E2%80%93309-38) On 6 December 1927, Colonel Juan Aberle (Chief of the Army Machine Shop) and Major Manuel Noguera (Deputy Chief of Police) presented an ultimatum to Romero demanding him to resign and accept the formation of a [military junta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Military_junta "Military junta") in exchange for safe passage out of El Salvador. Romero ordered both men to be arrested, and Aberle and Noguera were subsequently [court martialed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Court_martial "Court martial") and [executed by firing squad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Executed_by_firing_squad "Executed by firing squad") on 8 December 1927. A planned attack by 500 militants commanded by Jorge failed to support Aberle and Noguera as was planned. Hundreds of conspirators were arrested after the failed coup attempt, and Jorge fled the country to Honduras.[\[37\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P%C3%ADo_Romero_Bosque#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChing1997309%E2%80%93311-39) The coup's failure ended what remaining influence the Meléndez–Quiñónez dynasty had in Salvadoran politics.[\[38\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P%C3%ADo_Romero_Bosque#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChing1997311-40) As a result of the coup attempt, Romero re-implemented the state of emergency and press censorship until March 1929.[\[39\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P%C3%ADo_Romero_Bosque#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMolina2015-41)

[![Image 6: A headshot photograph portrait of Pío Romero Bosque](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/6b/Dr._Pio_Romero_Bosque.jpg/250px-Dr._Pio_Romero_Bosque.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Dr._Pio_Romero_Bosque.jpg)

Romero in c. 1923–1925[\[40\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P%C3%ADo_Romero_Bosque#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAndinoAndino1925iv-42)

At the start of Romero's presidency, coffee prices were high and El Salvador's coffee exports were at record highs.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P%C3%ADo_Romero_Bosque#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhite197397-4)[\[41\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P%C3%ADo_Romero_Bosque#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAstilla197630%E2%80%9331-43) Meanwhile, Romero inherited a budget deficit and [SV₡](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salvadoran_col%C3%B3n "Salvadoran colón")23.8 million of debt from his predecessor that resulted from issuing a high amount of fiscal bonds.[\[42\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P%C3%ADo_Romero_Bosque#cite_note-FOOTNOTECortez_Tejada2023141_&_144-44) In Romero's inaugural address, he stated that he intended to fix the country's financial situation. In 1927, he implemented several new taxes on imports to raise funding for the government and military. He also implemented a tax on all general stores operated by men in an effort to promote women's involvement in the economy.[\[43\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P%C3%ADo_Romero_Bosque#cite_note-FOOTNOTECortez_Tejada2023145-45) Romero granted tax exemptions on the cultivations of certain crops due to unrest from agricultural laborers regarding the tax rates.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P%C3%ADo_Romero_Bosque#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhite197397-4) International trade with Guatemala and Honduras was also granted exemptions from taxation.[\[44\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P%C3%ADo_Romero_Bosque#cite_note-FOOTNOTECortez_Tejada2023150-46) The Ministry of Finance reported that the reforms implemented in 1927 and 1928 had positive impacts on the country's economy as economic output increased.[\[45\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P%C3%ADo_Romero_Bosque#cite_note-FOOTNOTECortez_Tejada2023152%E2%80%93155-47)

In 1929, the [Great Depression](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Depression "Great Depression") led to the collapse of coffee prices, crippling El Salvador's economy as it was heavily reliant on coffee exports.[\[46\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P%C3%ADo_Romero_Bosque#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAstilla197631-48) Prices fell from SV₡‎39 per 100 pounds (45 kg) in 1928 to SV₡18 per 100 pounds by 1931. Wages also fell by over half of their pre-depression values. These economic conditions led to 80,000 laborers forming militant unions in western El Salvador that organized strikes and protests against Romero's government.[\[47\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P%C3%ADo_Romero_Bosque#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhite197399-49) Romero responded by outlawing rallies and demonstrations, and thousands were arrested.[\[48\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P%C3%ADo_Romero_Bosque#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhite197398-50)[\[49\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P%C3%ADo_Romero_Bosque#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWilsonLucero202481-51) By the end of Romero's presidency, El Salvador's debt stood at around US$4 million (equivalent to $82,704,595 in 2024).[\[50\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P%C3%ADo_Romero_Bosque#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAstilla197635-52)

Romero sought to implement democratic reforms in El Salvador, but historians are unsure what Romero's motives were as he never publicly gave a reason for doing so.[\[51\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P%C3%ADo_Romero_Bosque#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChing1997287_&_290%E2%80%93291-53) Scholar Patricia Alvarenga theorized that Romero may have implemented democratic reforms in order to combat the rising radicalization of laborers in the country.[\[52\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P%C3%ADo_Romero_Bosque#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChing1997292%E2%80%93293-54) Historian Erik Ching theorized that Romero "associated democracy with modernization" and wanted to "thrust El Salvador into the modern era".[\[53\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P%C3%ADo_Romero_Bosque#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChing1997302-55) Others suggest that Romero sought to appease the United States in order to maintain strong diplomatic and economic relations, or that Romero wanted to "leave his mark on history" by breaking with the pre-existing political system and establishing a new one.[\[54\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P%C3%ADo_Romero_Bosque#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChing1997302%E2%80%93303-56)

In May 1927, Romero proposed a constitutional amendment to implement a [secret ballot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Secret_ballot "Secret ballot"), but the amendment was never approved.[\[55\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P%C3%ADo_Romero_Bosque#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChing1997325%E2%80%93326-57) Romero dissolved the National Democratic Party on 6 September 1927 and prohibited anyone from claiming to be a member of the party in the December 1927 municipal elections, the first elections held during his presidency.[\[56\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P%C3%ADo_Romero_Bosque#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChing1997312%E2%80%93314-58) In an interview ahead of the election, Mendoza said that the government "does not favor any candidates anywhere; their government's interest is simply in guaranteeing liberty".[\[57\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P%C3%ADo_Romero_Bosque#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChing1997314%E2%80%93315-59) The election resulted in many former PND affiliates retaining power, but several municipalities did elect new candidates who were not affiliated with the PND.[\[58\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P%C3%ADo_Romero_Bosque#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChing1997323%E2%80%93324_&_514%E2%80%93515-60) The following month, the country held [legislative elections](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1928_Salvadoran_legislative_election "1928 Salvadoran legislative election") in which government-chosen candidates won every seat. Ching theorized that Romero did this to disallow his political opponents to potentially gain the power to impeach him.[\[59\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P%C3%ADo_Romero_Bosque#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChing1997340-61) The 1929 municipal elections saw more candidates who were never affiliated with the PND win seats, but many former PND candidates still held on to power.[\[60\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P%C3%ADo_Romero_Bosque#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChing1997346_&_519%E2%80%93520-62)

[![Image 7: A black-and-white photograph of Arturo Araujo's presidential inauguration](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/76/El_salvador_presidente_araujo_toma_la_presidencia_1930.jpg/250px-El_salvador_presidente_araujo_toma_la_presidencia_1930.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:El_salvador_presidente_araujo_toma_la_presidencia_1930.jpg)

Romero (third from the right) at [Arturo Araujo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arturo_Araujo "Arturo Araujo")'s (second from the right) 1931 presidential inauguration

In 1930, Romero announced that he would allow for new [political parties](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_political_parties_in_El_Salvador "List of political parties in El Salvador") to exist[\[49\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P%C3%ADo_Romero_Bosque#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWilsonLucero202481-51) on the condition that they did not seek to overthrow the government. Six political parties were soon formed.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P%C3%ADo_Romero_Bosque#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhite197397-4) Although Romero granted greater political freedoms, left-wing ideals were still prohibited[\[49\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P%C3%ADo_Romero_Bosque#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWilsonLucero202481-51) to the extent that the [Communist Party of El Salvador](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Communist_Party_of_El_Salvador "Communist Party of El Salvador") (PCES) had to be formed in secret.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P%C3%ADo_Romero_Bosque#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhite197397-4) From November 1930 to February 1931, around 1,200 people were imprisoned for left-wing political activity.[\[20\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P%C3%ADo_Romero_Bosque#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAnderson197141-20) Among those arrested was revolutionary [Farabundo Martí](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Farabundo_Mart%C3%AD "Farabundo Martí") whom Romero later had exiled from the country in December 1930.[\[48\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P%C3%ADo_Romero_Bosque#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhite197398-50)

Ahead of the [1931 presidential election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1931_Salvadoran_presidential_election "1931 Salvadoran presidential election"), Romero did not select a presidential successor,[\[61\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P%C3%ADo_Romero_Bosque#cite_note-FOOTNOTERacine1997234-63)[\[c\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P%C3%ADo_Romero_Bosque#cite_note-65) and as a result, several candidates participated in the election.[\[63\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P%C3%ADo_Romero_Bosque#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGrieb1971152-66) The _Diario del Salvador_ newspaper praised Romero's decision to not handpick a successor, writing that he had "broken forever with the traditions of the past" and referred to him as "El Salvador's greatest president".[\[62\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P%C3%ADo_Romero_Bosque#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAnderson197144-64) Among the candidates were Araujo and Zárate.[\[64\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P%C3%ADo_Romero_Bosque#cite_note-FOOTNOTENohlen2005287-67)[\[65\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P%C3%ADo_Romero_Bosque#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAstilla197634-68) Romero instructed polling officials to be impartial when counting votes.[\[48\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P%C3%ADo_Romero_Bosque#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhite197398-50) Araujo won the election with 46.7 percent of the vote in what historians considered to be the most free and fair election in Salvadoran history up to that point.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P%C3%ADo_Romero_Bosque#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHaggerty199014-2)[\[65\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P%C3%ADo_Romero_Bosque#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAstilla197634-68)[\[66\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P%C3%ADo_Romero_Bosque#cite_note-FOOTNOTENohlen2005270_&_287-69)

Romero left office on 1 March 1931 and was succeeded by Araujo.[\[67\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P%C3%ADo_Romero_Bosque#cite_note-FOOTNOTELeistenschneiderLeistenschneider1980185-70)[\[68\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P%C3%ADo_Romero_Bosque#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChing1997354-71)

[![Image 8: A black-and-white photograph of a family of five](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f9/P%C3%ADo_Romero_Bosque_and_his_family.png/250px-P%C3%ADo_Romero_Bosque_and_his_family.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:P%C3%ADo_Romero_Bosque_and_his_family.png)

Romero with his family (c. 1916)

Romero married Amparo Molina in 1891.[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P%C3%ADo_Romero_Bosque#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWard1916172-10) The couple had three children including [Pío Romero Bosque Molina](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=P%C3%ADo_Romero_Bosque_Molina&action=edit&redlink=1 "Pío Romero Bosque Molina (page does not exist)") and two daughters.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P%C3%ADo_Romero_Bosque#cite_note-FOOTNOTELeistenschneiderLeistenschneider1980183-5)[\[69\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P%C3%ADo_Romero_Bosque#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWard1916172%E2%80%93173-72) While Romero was president, his wife invited San Salvador's poor into the [Presidential Palace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Casa_Presidencial_/(El_Salvador/) "Casa Presidencial (El Salvador)") to celebrate his birthday.[\[70\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P%C3%ADo_Romero_Bosque#cite_note-FOOTNOTERacine1997223-73)

Later life and death
--------------------

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=P%C3%ADo_Romero_Bosque&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Later life and death")\]

[![Image 9: A photograph of Pío Romero Bosque's grave](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/ef/Tumba_De_Pio_Romero_Bosque._En_El_Cementerio_Los_Ilustes.jpg/250px-Tumba_De_Pio_Romero_Bosque._En_El_Cementerio_Los_Ilustes.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Tumba_De_Pio_Romero_Bosque._En_El_Cementerio_Los_Ilustes.jpg)

Romero's grave in the [Cemetery of Distinguished Citizens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cemetery_of_Distinguished_Citizens "Cemetery of Distinguished Citizens") in San Salvador

In December 1931, the Salvadoran military overthrew Araujo's government and installed his vice president, General [Maximiliano Hernández Martínez](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maximiliano_Hern%C3%A1ndez_Mart%C3%ADnez "Maximiliano Hernández Martínez"), as the country's provisional president.[\[71\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P%C3%ADo_Romero_Bosque#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChing1997363%E2%80%93364-74) Romero attempted to organize a political campaign to defeat Martínez in the [1935 presidential election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1935_Salvadoran_presidential_election "1935 Salvadoran presidential election"), but Romero fled the country in December 1933 for exile in Costa Rica after Martínez himself accused Romero of organizing a "communist sedition".[\[72\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P%C3%ADo_Romero_Bosque#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChing1997382%E2%80%93384-75) Romero had also come under heavy monitoring by the _orejas_ informant network.[\[73\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P%C3%ADo_Romero_Bosque#cite_note-FOOTNOTELindo_FuentesChingLara_Mart%C3%ADnez2007195-76) In a February 1934 interview with a U.S. military attaché, Romero denied plotting against Martínez.[\[74\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P%C3%ADo_Romero_Bosque#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChing1997384-77)

Romero died in Nicaragua on 10 December 1935.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P%C3%ADo_Romero_Bosque#cite_note-FOOTNOTELeistenschneiderLeistenschneider1980183-5)[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P%C3%ADo_Romero_Bosque#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMart%C3%ADnez_Pe%C3%B1ateS%C3%A1nchez2004461-6)[\[d\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P%C3%ADo_Romero_Bosque#cite_note-78) Martínez's government eventually reversed Romero's democratic reforms and El Salvador came under [undemocratic military rule](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Military_dictatorship_in_El_Salvador "Military dictatorship in El Salvador") for the next five decades.[\[75\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P%C3%ADo_Romero_Bosque#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChing1997356%E2%80%93358_&_490-79)

British author Alastair White described Romero's presidency as "the beginning of a period of transition ending with the suppression of the rebellion of 1932, after which the new order of things was apparent".[\[30\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P%C3%ADo_Romero_Bosque#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhite197395-32) American author Thomas P. Anderson wrote that Romero was remembered in El Salvador as "a kind of Salvadoran [Good King Wenceslaus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wenceslaus_I,_Duke_of_Bohemia "Wenceslaus I, Duke of Bohemia")" and described his presidency as a "golden age in the country's troubled history".[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P%C3%ADo_Romero_Bosque#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAnderson19718-3) Conversely, Salvadoran conservative editorialist Juan Ulloa blamed Romero's democratic reforms as directly causing _[La Matanza](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La_Matanza "La Matanza")_,[\[76\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P%C3%ADo_Romero_Bosque#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChingRam%C3%ADrez2017288-80) a 1932 rebellion led by Martí and the PCES followed up by the mass killings of up to 40,000 people.[\[77\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P%C3%ADo_Romero_Bosque#cite_note-FOOTNOTETulchinBland1992167-81) Ulloa also accused Romero of "knowing its \[communist\] leaders" ("_conoció sus lideres \[comunistas\]_").[\[76\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P%C3%ADo_Romero_Bosque#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChingRam%C3%ADrez2017288-80)

El Salvador's Military Massacres Civilians
------------------------------------------

**Date** January-February, 1932

_The massacre of up to thirty thousand peasants by the Salvadoran army ended a radical reform movement in the countryside and ushered in fifty years of repression and military rule in El Salvador._

**Locale** El Salvador

Key Figures
-----------

*   Agustín Farabundo Martí (1893-1932), principal leader of the Salvadoran Communist Party
*   Maximiliano Hernández Martínez (1882-1966), military dictator of El Salvador, 1931-1944
*   Arturo Araújo (1877-1967), president of El Salvador, March-December, 1931

Summary of Event
----------------

Social relations in El Salvador in the first decades of the twentieth century were characterized by a wide division in power. The peasant masses, who had once enjoyed communal property rights as part of an ancient landholding system, had seen these rights taken away in the late 1800’s by a powerful clique of coffee planters. Behind a shield of “liberal” legislation, these growers had succeeded in expanding their holdings to encompass nearly all of the country’s arable land. They modernized the economy by tying their fortunes to the exclusive cultivation of coffee, for which a large international market existed.

The peasants, most of whom were Pipil Indians, had an almost mystical reverence for their cornfields. The disestablishment of their communal system had a psychological as well as a material effect on their lives. Without access to land, they had no options other than to work on the coffee plantations as _colonos_, receiving in exchange tiny plots for their own subsistence along with miserable wages, often issued in kind. Once-independent peasants were thus reduced to debt peons.

For their part, the members of the coffee growers’ oligarchy took advantage of a seemingly limitless world demand for their product. The coffee boom, which lasted throughout the 1920’s, stimulated urbanization, brought railways and telegraph lines to the interior, and widened the economic gap between the oligarchs and the peasantry. The wealthy lived in regal splendor while the poor seethed in their poverty.

The rural environment of El Salvador had little in it of philanthropy. The planters kept wages low, and they paid almost no taxes that might support social services. As a consequence, discontent among the poor was widespread, and isolated uprisings occurred frequently. The rural constabulary and the national guard crushed all of these movements. As time went by, the oligarchs came to rely more and more on coercion to maintain the status quo in the countryside.

The coming of the [Great Depression](https://www.ebsco.com/research-starters/history/halifax-explosion) in 1929 provided the catalyst for a social explosion. The demand for coffee on the world markets collapsed. With prices falling, the _colonos_ lost the opportunity to find work. Wages fell 60 percent. In the cities, the Depression gave rise to a period of intense political discussion, with younger members of the oligarchy expressing some doubts as to whether the traditional order could contain the social crisis. A few individuals looked to reformist solutions.

Among their number was Arturo Araújo, an admirer of Britain’s Fabian Socialists. Araújo was something of a wild card in Salvadoran politics, and the Partido Laborista he founded reflected an eclectic blend of mysticism, anti-imperialism, and what was termed _vitalismo mínimo–_the idea that every citizen deserved a “vital minimum” of goods and services necessary to a happy life. Such sentiments appealed to many, especially in the cities, where trade unionists and middle-class professionals lent avid support to Araújo.

The Communist Party of El Salvador also favored this wayward son of the oligarchy. In this instance, however, the party’s support was conditional, because the Communists, led by veteran activist Agustín Farabundo Martí, feared that Araújo’s popularity might overshadow their own plans to carve a measure of power from the country’s difficulties. As it turned out, they needed to fear something far more sinister.

Despite the misgivings of most oligarchs, the government held free elections in January, 1931. Five presidential candidates, most of whom represented conservative coffee interests, entered the field against Araújo. The latter went on to win anyway and took office at the beginning of March. Problems plagued Araújo from the beginning. The Depression hit the country people very hard. Although he had made vague promises as to land reform, the new president simply could not deliver on these while simultaneously safeguarding the privileges of the elite.

The lack of direction displayed by Araújo was evident from the beginning. The oligarchs, who had previously thought Araújo merely risky, now saw him as positively dangerous and looked to anyone who might deliver them from his influences. The peasants and the trade unionists also became disillusioned. Seeing that their support had brought them repression and not reform, they began to consider more radical solutions, particularly those espoused by Farabundo Martí and the Communists. Several strikes by _colonos_ in April and May were brutally put down by forces under War Minister (and Vice President) Maximiliano Hernández Martínez. Widespread rebellion now seemed likely.

Of all the groups opposed to Araújo, clearly the most willing to act on its grievances was the military. The president had tried to reduce the army’s budget by 25 percent and tried to retire a number of senior officers. Most crucial, however, was his inability to pay his soldiers. In normal times, export duties paid the greater part of government expenses, but with coffee exports at rock bottom, Araújo’s administration was delinquent in its payments to all officials.

The end came swiftly. On December 2, 1931, army units loyal to General Hernández Martínez seized control of San Salvador and other major cities. Only Araújo loyalists initially condemned the attack. Most political parties, including the Communists, gave their tacit approval. They felt reassured when Hernández Martínez announced that municipal elections scheduled for January, 1932, would go forward. The Left then organized meetings and street demonstrations, distributed leaflets, and prepared for the elections. Few doubted that Hernández Martínez would keep his word.

The general, however, had his own ambitions. A man of a mystical frame of mind who would later conduct seances in the presidential palace, he felt certain that he acted with divine aid. Having identified all opposition organizers, he cancelled the elections and began a massive repression. Realizing that they were moving in the eleventh hour, the Communists launched an urban revolt on January 22, supposedly set to coincide with a rural insurrection in the western departments of Santa Ana, Ahuachapán, and Sonsonate. The Indian leaders of those areas had tenuous ties to Farabundo Martí, even though they had no use for Communists generally. They nevertheless decided that a revolt offered them their last chance of deliverance.

They were wrong, tragically so. The army quelled the urban uprising in a matter of hours, police agents having already penetrated the revolutionary cells. They had previously detained Farabundo Martí. A policy of summary execution began that included even suspected members of opposition groups. Martí received unusual treatment: He was given a brief trial before he faced the firing squad.

The rural districts experienced the full fury of the repression. The peasant rebels, armed with machetes, managed to hold out for forty-eight hours. They killed some fifty policemen. The army and the irregular forces set up by the landowners exacted an awesome revenge in what Salvadorans still refer to simply as _la matanza_, the massacre. The army regarded anyone with Indian features as being automatically guilty and liable for the ultimate penalty. Whole villages were razed. Hospitals were checked and the wounded dragged out and killed. Women, children, and dogs were shot along with men. The corpses soon became so numerous that they could not be buried and were simply left in ditches along the roads. As one witness later observed, only the vultures ate well that year. Before the violence had run its course in February, as many as thirty thousand people had died. The massacre left a legacy of violence in Salvadoran politics that was overcome only decades later.

Significance
------------

_La matanza_ left a deep scar in Salvadoran society. Virtually every family in the western part of the country lost someone to the army terror. The effects of the repression went even further, however, than the loss of life. There were cultural losses. Because Hernández Martínez and the army chose to identify the Pipil Indians as part of a wide Communist conspiracy, most Indian survivors rushed to deny their Indian identity. They abandoned the use of native garb, which they saw as a provocative symbol of resistance likely to bring down the wrath of the police. Indians encouraged their children to avoid speaking Pipil except at home, and then only in hushed tones.

There were social losses. With the members of many families serving in the army or among the rebels, the repression could not help but have a divisive impact. It became impossible to trust anyone. All of the traditional foci of rural authority and trust—the church and, more important, the socioreligious brotherhoods (_cofradías_)—lost the popular support they once had enjoyed. Fear dominated the peasant landscape. Only the oligarchs could claim that _la matanza_ had increased the level of solidarity in their ranks. It also taught them the false lesson that class solidarity outweighed national reconciliation and that their survival depended on the subordination of the peasants.

Finally, the repression brought political losses. General Hernández Martínez followed _la matanza_ with a twelve-year [dictatorship](https://www.ebsco.com/research-starters/political-science/dictatorship) that brooked little opposition, even from the oligarchs. Although civilian vigilantes conducted much of the 1932 slaughter, that event’s political outcome confirmed the army’s claim on power. Hernández Martínez was only one of many military presidents who were to rule El Salvador during the twentieth century. As an institution, the Salvadoran armed forces consistently resisted pressures to make room for civilian participation in politics. When open application of force was inadvisable, the military acted in collusion with the oligarchs to create death squads.

For their part, the peasant masses in El Salvador became caught between two polar extremes in the late twentieth century. They could either join the ranks of the army and the elites, who perceived the struggle as an anti-Communist crusade, or they could join with the Farabundo Martí National Liberation Front (FMLN) guerrillas, the ideological descendants of Martí, and fight to establish the kind of Leninist regime that had been repudiated throughout the Eastern Bloc. In either direction, death threatened the average citizen. The greatest and most frightening legacies of _la matanza_ were the effects that it left in the popular mind and the knowledge that it could happen again. However, a peace settlement reached in 1992 between the Salvadoran government and the FMLN paved the way for these fears to be alleviated in a spirit of national reconciliation and a new democratic process for a nation too long torn by civil war.

Bibliography
------------

Anderson, Thomas P. _Matanza_. 2d ed. Willimantic, Conn.: Curbstone Press, 1992. Considered the classic English-language account of the repression. Thoughtful treatment draws on extensive interviews with participants and previously little-known manuscript materials. Includes map, footnotes, extensive bibliography, and index.

Dalton, Roque. _Miguel Marmol_. Willimantic, Conn.: Curbstone Press, 1987. Unique and fascinating account of _la matanza_ based on extensive interviews with an active organizer of the Salvadoran Communist Party who was himself shot and left for dead in 1932 and who later spent many years in exile in the Soviet Union. Marmol’s Stalinist attitude dates him, but his comments about sacrifice and struggle still ring true. Dalton, an important poet and member of the revolutionary underground, was murdered in 1975 by a rival leftist faction. Includes three letters from Marmol as well as an October, 1986, interview.

Holden, Robert H. _Armies Without Nations: Public Violence and State Formation in Central America, 1821-1960_. New York: Oxford University Press, 2004. Examines how Central American states have exercised public violence as a way of maintaining authority. Includes discussion of _la matanza_ in El Salvador. Features photographs, endnotes, and index.

McClintock, Michael. _State Terror and Popular Resistance in El Salvador_. Vol. 1 in _The American Connection_. London: Zed Books, 1985. Thorough examination of U.S. military and economic aid to El Salvador contains some useful information on the 1932 massacre, including some of the comments of the American military attaché in San Salvador at the time. Includes endnotes, bibliography, and index.

Montgomery, Tommie Sue. _Revolution in El Salvador: From Civil Strife to Civil Peace_. 2d ed. Boulder, Colo.: Westview Press, 1995. Insightful history of the Salvadoran struggle for justice focuses more on the 1970’s and 1980’s than on _la matanza_ but provides a detailed account of the antecedents of the quagmire of the 1990’s, making it a key source for those seeking to understand modern El Salvador. Includes photos, maps, tables, bibliography, and index.

North, Liisa. _Bitter Grounds: Roots of Revolt in El Salvador_. 2d ed. Westport, Conn.: Lawrence Hill, 1985. Brief but concise treatment of Salvadoran politics in the twentieth century, especially strong concerning economic questions. Chapter 3 covers the 1932 peasant revolt and its bloody aftermath. Includes maps, tables, notes, bibliography, appendixes, and index.

Parkman, Patricia. _Nonviolent Insurrection in El Salvador: The Fall of Maximiliano Hernández Martínez_. Tucson: University of Arizona Press, 1988. Valuable, well-researched account of the Hernández Martínez regime focuses more on his ouster in the mid-1940’s than on _la matanza_. Based largely on materials drawn from the archives of the U.S. Department of State and on interviews. Includes maps, illustrations, endnotes, and bibliography.

Russell, Philip L. _El Salvador in Crisis_. Austin, Tex.: Colorado River Press, 1984. Like most “committed” historical works, this study favors a leftist solution for the Salvadoran problem. Provides a thorough treatment of the 1932 bloodbath. Includes maps, tables, illustrations, graphs, endnotes, bibliography, and index.

La **elección presidencial de El Salvador de 1923** fue llevada a cabo el 14 de enero de 1923. [Alfonso Quiñónez Molina](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfonso_Qui%C3%B1%C3%B3nez_Molina "Alfonso Quiñónez Molina") era el único candidato y ganó las elecciones.[\[1\]](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elecci%C3%B3n_presidencial_de_El_Salvador_de_1923#cite_note-1)​ Gobierno de Jorge Meléndez -------------------------- \[[editar](https://es.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Elecci%C3%B3n_presidencial_de_El_Salvador_de_1923&action=edit§ion=1 "Editar sección: Gobierno de Jorge Meléndez")\] La [Dinastía Melendez Quiñonez](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dinast%C3%ADa_Mel%C3%A9ndez-Qui%C3%B1ones "Dinastía Meléndez-Quiñones") que inicio tras el asesinato del Presidente [Manuel Enrique Araujo](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manuel_Enrique_Araujo "Manuel Enrique Araujo") tenía la tradición de dar el cargo [presidencial](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presidencialismo "Presidencialismo") usando el [Nepotismo](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nepotismo "Nepotismo") como herramienta principal para dicha acción, la dinastía empezó con el presidente [Carlos Meléndez](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carlos_Mel%C3%A9ndez_/(pol%C3%ADtico/) "Carlos Meléndez (político)") un [latifundista](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latifundio "Latifundio") de las familias cafetaleras en [El Salvador](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Salvador "El Salvador"), que tras su [fallecimiento](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fallecimiento "Fallecimiento") su [hermano](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hermano "Hermano") [Jorge Meléndez](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jorge_Mel%C3%A9ndez_Ram%C3%ADrez "Jorge Meléndez Ramírez") lo sustituyó en el cargo presidencial continuando las [políticas](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pol%C3%ADticas_p%C3%BAblicas "Políticas públicas") de su antecesor, Para 1922 [Jorge Meléndez](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jorge_Mel%C3%A9ndez_Ram%C3%ADrez "Jorge Meléndez Ramírez") tuvo que enfrentar altos [escándalos](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Esc%C3%A1ndalos "Escándalos") de [corrupción](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corrupci%C3%B3n_pol%C3%ADtica "Corrupción política"), [déficit económicos](https://es.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=D%C3%A9ficit_econ%C3%B3micos&action=edit&redlink=1 "Déficit económicos (aún no redactado)"),desastres naturales y bajos aumentos salariales a empleados públicos a la vez tuvo lidiar con la [deuda externa](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deuda_externa "Deuda externa") heredada de la [federación centroamericana](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Provincias_Unidas_del_Centro_de_Am%C3%A9rica "Provincias Unidas del Centro de América") fue así que el gobierno de Melendez tuvo que hacer [millonarios](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Millonario "Millonario") [préstamos](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pr%C3%A9stamos "Préstamos") y [contratos de arrendamiento](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Contrato_de_arrendamiento "Contrato de arrendamiento") hacia los [puertos marítimos,](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Puerto "Puerto") y [transportes ferroviarios](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferroviario "Ferroviario") con durabilidad de 15 años hacia los [Bancos Estadounidenses](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Banco "Banco") y la [United Fruit Company](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Fruit_Company "United Fruit Company"), esto provocó manifestaciones a nivel nacional las cuales terminaron siendo reprimidas por la [Policía Nacional](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cuerpos_de_Seguridad_/(El_Salvador/) "Cuerpos de Seguridad (El Salvador)"). Candidatura de Miguel Tomas Molina ---------------------------------- \[[editar](https://es.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Elecci%C3%B3n_presidencial_de_El_Salvador_de_1923&action=edit§ion=2 "Editar sección: Candidatura de Miguel Tomas Molina")\] El 25 de diciembre de 1922 en las cercanías entre la Iglesia El Calvario y el Mercado Central en [San Salvador](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Salvador "San Salvador"), un grupo de mujeres se manifestó en contra de la candidatura del [Dr](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doctorado "Doctorado"). [Alfonso Quiñonez Molina](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfonso_Qui%C3%B1%C3%B3nez_Molina "Alfonso Quiñónez Molina") ya que pretendía seguir con las políticas de la dinastía familiar y propondrían al [Dr](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doctorado "Doctorado"). [Miguel Tomas Molina](https://es.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Miguel_Tomas_Molina&action=edit&redlink=1 "Miguel Tomas Molina (aún no redactado)") como candidato opositor a la [Dinastía Meléndez Quiñonez](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dinast%C3%ADa_Mel%C3%A9ndez-Qui%C3%B1ones "Dinastía Meléndez-Quiñones"), Molina era [abogado](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abogado "Abogado") de profesión graduado en la [Universidad de El Salvador](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universidad_de_El_Salvador "Universidad de El Salvador") además tenía vinculación familiar con el presidente Quiñonez, como primo en consanginidad se desempeñó como férreo opositor hacia la familia Meléndez Quiñonez, lamentablemente esta manifestación terminó siendo reprimida por la [Guardia Nacional](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guardia_Nacional_/(El_Salvador/) "Guardia Nacional (El Salvador)") y La Liga Roja que era un grupo paramilitar creado por Quiñones para vigilar a la oposición la manifestación terminó con un saldo de [víctimas](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/V%C3%ADctimas "Víctimas") desconocido, algunas personas pudieron refugiarse en el hospicio de varones que colindaba con la iglesia el calvario, Quiñonez terminó ganando la elección tres semanas después en esta [manifestación](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manifestaci%C3%B3n "Manifestación") se destaca la participación de [Prudencia Ayala](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prudencia_Ayala "Prudencia Ayala") a los 37 años de edad. 1. [↑](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elecci%C3%B3n_presidencial_de_El_Salvador_de_1923#cite_ref-1) [\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salvadoran_presidential_election,_1923)
